Existing insurance TPs address premium diversion (TP-0005) and disability fraud (TP-0010), but not the core motor/medical false claims pattern that represents the highest-volume insurance fraud globally. The government sector inclusion reflects that Medicare/Medicaid (US) and equivalent national health programs are targeted by the same false claims pattern applied to public payers.

item.title: [TP-0057] Deepfake-as-a-Service Marketplace Ecosystem
item.description:
Deepfake-as-a-Service (DaaS) platforms operating on dark web marketplaces and Telegram that provide subscription-based access to deepfake generation tools — voice cloning, real-time face swapping, AI face/voice changers, and synthetic media production. UNODC documents a 600% surge in deepfake mentions across criminal Telegram channels with 10+ active vendor ecosystems serving Southeast Asian scam compounds. Group-IB confirms voice clones can be generated from as little as 10 seconds of target audio. Flare/IBM X-Force documents DPRK IT worker operatives using AI face/voice changers during live video interviews to impersonate Western identities. Pricing ranges from $100–$1,000/month subscriptions to per-use voice clone API calls.
**Distinction from TP-0007**: TP-0007 covers the fraud execution pattern of deepfake voice authorization for wire transfers; TP-0057 covers the upstream *marketplace and tooling ecosystem* that produces and distributes the deepfake capabilities used in TP-0007 and other fraud types.

item.title: [TP-0058] Scam Compound Operational Infrastructure
item.description:
Operational fraud mechanics inside industrialized scam compounds. UNODC documents $40B annual profits from scam compound operations, with multilingual AI chatbots deployed for automated victim engagement and bot-driven operational scaling. INTERPOL reports 80 nationalities trafficked into compound operations, with geographic expansion from Southeast Asia into MENA and Africa. Compounds operate as industrial fraud factories with professional management hierarchies, performance metrics, shift-based operations, CRM systems tracking victim "portfolios," and scripted sextortion fallback playbooks when investment scam conversion stalls.
**Distinction from TP-0047**: TP-0047 covers the human trafficking and physical infrastructure nexus enabling compound existence; TP-0058 covers the operational fraud mechanics, management structures, and technology stack deployed inside compounds to execute fraud at scale.
The World Cybercrime Index (Bruce et al., PLoS ONE 2024) provides partial geographic context: China ranks #3 globally (WCI 27.86) with significant cash-out/money laundering scores (24.13), supporting the documented role of Chinese Money Laundering Networks (CMLNs) in scam compound monetization. However, WCI data was collected in 2021, predating the explosive growth of SE Asian scam compounds (2022+) — Cambodia, Myanmar, and Laos are absent from WCI rankings despite being primary operational bases by 2025-2026.

item.title: [TP-0059] Automated Mule Account Infrastructure
item.description:
Bot-driven mule account creation and management infrastructure that automates the opening, maintenance, and coordination of money mule accounts at scale. UNODC documents bot-driven mule account systems integrated into scam compound laundering operations. Recorded Future identifies automated KYC circumvention toolkits on dark web marketplaces that combine synthetic identity documents, liveness check bypass tools, and device emulators to open accounts across multiple financial institutions simultaneously. INTERPOL reports mule networks comprising thousands of accounts per operation, enabling rapid layering of fraud proceeds across jurisdictions.
**Distinction from TP-0049**: TP-0049 covers the downstream cryptocurrency laundering techniques; TP-0059 covers the upstream automated infrastructure that creates and manages the mule accounts used as the first layer of laundering.
The geographic distribution of money mule networks aligns with WCI (Bruce et al., PLoS ONE 2024) cash-out/money laundering scores: the US (26.63/100) and UK (21.63) rank as the top Western cash-out jurisdictions, reflecting their role as primary mule account destinations rather than fraud production hubs. Note: WCI data was collected in 2021.

item.title: [TP-0060] Investment Fraud TDS Pipeline
item.description:
Traffic Distribution Systems (TDS) weaponized specifically for investment fraud delivery — routing potential victims from legitimate advertising platforms through multi-hop cloaking chains to fraudulent investment platforms. Recorded Future documents TDS infrastructure as a critical fraud-enabling service exploited by investment scam operators. Infoblox identifies specific RDGA actors (Reckless Rabbit, Ruthless Rabbit, Savvy Seahorse) operating TDS infrastructure that routes victims based on geolocation, device fingerprint, and behavioral profile. Commercial TDS platforms (Keitaro, Binom) are abused for traffic cloaking and geo-routing, showing compliant content to security researchers while routing real victims to scam investment platforms.
**Distinction from TP-0042**: TP-0042 covers TDS chain exploitation broadly across fraud types; TP-0060 covers the specific investment fraud TDS pipeline — from advertising click to fake investment platform — with emphasis on the investment-specific cloaking, victim qualification, and platform routing techniques.

item.title: [TP-0061] Threat Actor Enabling Bulletproof Hosting Infrastructure
item.description:
Bulletproof hosting (BPH) providers and abuse-resistant infrastructure services that enable fraud operations by providing hosting that resists takedown requests, law enforcement cooperation, and abuse complaints. Recorded Future identifies specific providers — Virtualine, Stark Industries, AEZA, Aurologic — as Threat Actor Enabling (TAE) entities operating from jurisdictions with weak enforcement. INTERPOL Operation Shadow Storm targeted fraud-enabling infrastructure providers. These TAE entities provide the foundational hosting layer for TDS infrastructure, fake investment platforms, DaaS platforms, mule account management systems, and FaaS marketplaces — making them a critical enabling dependency across multiple fraud threat paths.
**Distinction from TP-0044**: TP-0044 covers the broader state-criminal infrastructure convergence pattern; TP-0061 focuses specifically on the commercial bulletproof hosting providers that sell abuse-resistant infrastructure to fraud operators as a business model.

item.title: [TP-0062] Recovery Fraud — Double-Dip Re-victimization
item.description:
Recovery fraud is an organized crime model in which victims of prior fraud (investment scams, romance fraud, pig butchering) are systematically re-contacted by actors posing as asset recovery agents, lawyers, law enforcement officials, or government bodies who claim they can recover the victim's lost funds — for an upfront fee. The UNODC identifies this as a distinct organized fraud operation with separate infrastructure from the initial fraud, targeting an identifiable victim population using traded "lead lists" of prior fraud complainants. Recovery fraud exploits the emotional vulnerability and financial desperation of already-defrauded individuals, often resulting in substantial secondary losses.
**Distinction from upstream TPs**: TP-0011 (Romance Scam) and TP-0017 (Pig Butchering) document the initial fraud schemes. TP-0062 documents the distinct second-stage organized crime operation that re-targets those same victims through entirely separate infrastructure and impersonation narratives.

item.title: [TP-0063] Organized Counterfeit Goods and Non-Delivery Fraud Networks
item.description:
Organized criminal groups operate networks of fraudulent e-commerce websites, fake sellers on legitimate auction platforms, and counterfeit goods supply chains to defraud consumers at scale. The UNODC documents this as the most prevalent fraud category by volume, with OCGs running multi-site operations backed by dedicated money laundering infrastructure, recruited money mules, and counterfeit supply chains linked to traditional organized crime. Distinct from individual purchase scams, the organized dimension involves supply chain structures mimicking legitimate businesses, coordinated use of stolen identities for seller accounts, cross-border money laundering, and the deliberate exploitation of legitimate platform trust mechanisms.
**Distinction from TP-0036/TP-0030**: TP-0036 (Purchase Scam Merchant Networks) covers individual scam merchant tactics. TP-0030 (E-Commerce Triangulation) covers triangulation fraud. TP-0063 documents the organized crime infrastructure behind multi-site consumer fraud networks — the OCG structures, the supply chains, and the money laundering operations that UNODC identifies as organized criminal groups under UNTOC.

item.title: [TP-0064] Long-Firm and Organized Business Credit Fraud
item.description:
Long-firm fraud and organized financial statement fraud involve OCGs establishing or acquiring legitimate businesses, building creditworthiness over months or years, then exploiting that trust to defraud supply chain partners, trade finance banks, or investors. The UNODC identifies this as a distinct organized crime category where criminals build companies specifically for the purpose of large-scale credit fraud, often facilitated by professional enablers (accountants, lawyers, mortgage brokers, real estate appraisers). Distinguished from credit card bust-outs by the scale, duration, and corporate structure involved — UNODC case studies document single operations defrauding 20+ banks across multiple countries for $500M+.
**Distinction from TP-0003/TP-0019**: TP-0003 (Synthetic Identity Bust-Out) covers synthetic identity-driven credit card bust-outs. TP-0019 (Business Identity Theft) covers theft of existing business identities. TP-0064 documents the UNODC long-firm model: building a real business with real credit history, then exploiting that earned trust for organized large-scale fraud.

item.title: [TP-0065] Organized Mass-Marketing Fraud Infrastructure (Boiler Rooms & Lead Lists)
item.description:
Organized mass-marketing fraud infrastructure encompasses the boiler room operations, lead list ecosystems, robodialling infrastructure, and SIM farm devices that serve as the shared demand-generation engine feeding multiple downstream fraud types. The UNODC identifies mass-marketing as a cross-cutting facilitator of organized fraud, documenting call center operations (boiler rooms) that employ salaried agents, use "lead lists" of targeted victims (including "suckers lists" of previously defrauded individuals), and leverage telecommunications infrastructure (SIM farms, VoIP spoofing, robodialling) for high-volume victim contact. This infrastructure operates as a discrete business layer — separate from the fraud execution itself — and may serve multiple fraud types simultaneously (investment scams, impersonation, recovery fraud, tech support fraud).
**Distinction from TP-0058**: TP-0058 (Scam Compound Operations) covers the physical compound model in South-East Asia where trafficked individuals perpetrate fraud. TP-0065 documents the broader mass-marketing infrastructure layer that UNODC identifies as a cross-cutting facilitator across all regions — including virtual boiler rooms, offshore call centers, and the lead list/robodialling ecosystem that enables organized fraud at scale.

item.title: [TP-0066] Crash-for-Cash and Organized Insurance Fraud Rings
item.description:
Crash-for-cash fraud involves organized criminal groups that systematically stage or cause vehicle accidents to generate fraudulent insurance claims. The UNODC identifies this as a distinct organized crime activity under fraud against businesses/organizations, where OCGs recruit designated drivers, participants who claim injuries, and corrupt professional enablers (medical practitioners, lawyers, repair shops) to submit coordinated fraudulent claims. In more serious cases, OCGs deliberately cause accidents involving innocent members of the public to increase claim legitimacy. The organized dimension includes recruitment networks, shared medical/legal professionals across multiple staged incidents, and systematic claim submission infrastructure.
**Distinction from TP-0056**: TP-0056 (Insurance Claims Fraud) covers individual fraudulent claims including document forgery and exaggerated claims. TP-0066 documents the organized ring dimension: coordinated multi-participant staged incidents, shared professional enabler networks, and OCG structures managing multiple fraudulent accident campaigns.

item.title: [TP-0067] AiTM Phishing Kit Infrastructure and Session Token Hijacking
item.description:
Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing kits represent the most significant evolution in credential theft infrastructure, enabling attackers to bypass multi-factor authentication by proxying victim sessions through attacker-controlled infrastructure in real time. The attacker captures both credentials and session tokens/cookies as the victim authenticates with the legitimate service. Sekoia.io identified 11 major AiTM phishing kits active in early 2025, with Tycoon 2FA as the most prevalent (1,200+ domains, targeting 500K+ organizations monthly). Credential phishing attacks surged 703% in H2 2024. These kits operate as Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) marketplaces, lowering the barrier to sophisticated MFA-bypass attacks. FIDO2/phishing-resistant MFA blocks 93.9% of AiTM campaigns, making it the primary defensive recommendation.
**Distinction from TP-0054**: TP-0054 (FaaS Ecosystem) covers the broader fraud-as-a-service model. TP-0067 focuses specifically on the AiTM phishing kit infrastructure — the reverse proxy technology, session token capture mechanics, and PhaaS distribution model that enables downstream BEC, account takeover, and wire fraud.

item.title: [TP-0068] Gift Card Fraud Lifecycle — Generation, Tampering, and Monetization
item.description:
Gift card fraud encompasses a comprehensive attack lifecycle documented by the NRF Retail Fraud Taxonomy: brute-force number generation or purchase of stolen card numbers, automated balance probing to identify funded cards, physical tampering of unactivated cards in retail locations, card merging to consolidate illicit value, gift card extortion (impersonating government officials to coerce victims into purchasing cards), and monetization via resale platforms and drop shipping. This threat path is distinct from account takeover paths to gift card theft (TP-0013) — it covers the full gift card-centric fraud chain where the card itself is the primary target, not the account. The NRF documents this as a primary scheme involving organized theft groups (OTGs) operating at scale.
**Distinction from TP-0013**: TP-0013 covers credential stuffing to loyalty/gift card account drain (the ATO path). TP-0068 covers the NRF RFT's gift card fraud lifecycle where the card is targeted directly through generation, tampering, balance probing, and extortion — without necessarily requiring account compromise.

item.title: [TP-0069] Smishing PhaaS Ecosystem — Darcula, Smishing Triad, and Mass-Messaging Credential Harvest
item.description:
The Smishing PhaaS Ecosystem is a loosely federated Chinese-speaking cybercrime network — collectively known as the Smishing Triad — that operates industrialized smishing infrastructure at unprecedented scale: 194,000+ malicious domains registered since January 2024, 884,000+ credit cards compromised in a seven-month period, and victims in 121+ countries. The ecosystem centers on three major Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) platforms — Darcula (tracked as LARVA-246), Lucid (operated by XinXin Group / LARVA-242), and Lighthouse (developed by Wang Duo Yu / LARVA-241) — supported by independent kit developers (Chenlun), bulk SMS enablers (Oak Tel/Carrie SMS), and dedicated smishing message platforms (Panda Shop, StupidFISH). What distinguishes this threat path from traditional SMS phishing is the exploitation of Apple iMessage and Android RCS to bypass carrier-level SMS filtering, real-time character-by-character credential streaming via Magic Cat, and the integration of GenAI-powered phishing form generation (darcula-suite 3.0). FBI IC3 received 59,271 toll-scam complaints in 2024 alone, reflecting the scale of the toll/road fee lure campaign impersonating E-ZPass, SunPass, FasTrak, and I-Pass across 8+ U.S. states.
**Distinction from TP-0067**: TP-0067 covers AiTM phishing kit infrastructure focused on session token hijacking and MFA bypass via reverse proxy. TP-0069 covers the smishing delivery ecosystem — the SMS/iMessage/RCS-based credential harvest pipeline, the PhaaS platforms that power it, and the supporting bulk messaging and kit development infrastructure specific to mobile messaging channels.

item.title: [TP-0070] Travel Booking Fraud & Fake OTA Networks
item.description: Travel booking fraud and fake Online Travel Agency (OTA) networks represent a rapidly growing fraud category, with estimated global losses reaching $37 billion through Buy-for-You (B4U) services alone. Fraudsters operate fake travel agency websites mimicking legitimate OTAs (Booking.com, Expedia, Airbnb), with 4,344 fake travel domains identified in active campaigns. Telegram-based B4U agencies offer deeply discounted travel bookings purchased with stolen payment credentials, creating a laundering layer between cardholders and travel providers. The ecosystem encompasses fake OTA domains, vacation rental hijacking, loyalty point laundering (TP-0013), and AI-enhanced scam operations that generate convincing travel listings and customer service interactions. Seasonal peaks align with holiday booking periods, amplifying losses during Q4 and summer travel seasons.

item.title: [TP-0071] IRSF & Telecom Revenue Share Fraud
item.description: International Revenue Share Fraud (IRSF) is the single largest category of telecommunications fraud, generating $10.76 billion in annual losses according to the CFCA/TNS Global Fraud Loss Survey (2026). IRSF exploits the inter-carrier settlement system where originating carriers pay terminating carriers per-minute rates for international calls. Fraudsters establish revenue-sharing agreements with premium-rate number providers in high-rate destinations, then generate artificial call traffic to those numbers using compromised PBX systems, SIM boxes, or automated dialers. Wangiri ("one-ring") fraud, a variant where victims are tricked into calling back premium-rate numbers, adds a social engineering dimension. The convergence of SIM box fraud (TP-0008), compromised enterprise PBX systems, and sophisticated traffic routing creates a multi-layered ecosystem that is difficult to detect in real time. Machine learning-based detection has achieved 98% accuracy in identifying IRSF traffic patterns.

item.title: [TP-0072] Telecom Subscription & Billing Fraud
item.description: Telecom subscription and billing fraud encompasses the use of stolen, synthetic, or manipulated identities to fraudulently obtain telecom services, devices, and credit -- combined with unauthorized billing manipulation that charges victims for premium services they never requested. TransUnion reports that 53% of telecom executives identify subscription fraud as their top concern, driven by the increasing sophistication of synthetic identity creation (TP-0003) and GenAI-powered KYC bypass techniques. The total telecom fraud ecosystem reaches $41.82B annually (CFCA/TNS 2026), with subscription fraud as a primary entry point that enables downstream fraud including device resale, SIM swap attacks (TP-0008), and premium SMS billing schemes (cramming). GenAI tools now generate convincing synthetic identity documents that pass automated KYC checks, enabling fraudsters to open multiple telecom accounts for device acquisition at industrial scale.

item.title: [TP-0073] Real Estate Title Fraud & Deed Theft
item.description: Real estate title fraud and deed theft represent a growing category of property-related fraud, with FBI data reporting $16.6 billion in total real estate fraud losses in 2024. The core scheme involves impersonating property owners -- primarily targeting vacant lots, unencumbered properties, and absentee-owner homes -- to fraudulently transfer titles or initiate sales, diverting proceeds to attacker-controlled accounts. The emergence of AI-forged documents (deeds, government IDs, notary stamps) and deepfake video notarization has dramatically lowered the barrier to executing these schemes, with Entrust reporting a 40% year-over-year increase in deepfake-related fraud attempts. Seller impersonation of vacant property owners is the most common vector, as these properties lack occupants who would notice unauthorized activity. Virginia's 2025 deed fraud legislation represents the first major legislative response, mandating enhanced identity verification for property transfers. This threat path intersects with wire fraud (TP-0006) at the monetization phase, where sale proceeds are redirected via business email compromise or fraudulent wire instructions.

item.title: [TP-0074] Ghost Broking & Unauthorized Insurance Portals
item.description:
Ghost broking is a rapidly growing insurance fraud typology where unlicensed individuals or organized crime groups sell fraudulent, forged, or illegitimately obtained motor insurance policies to unsuspecting consumers. Victims increased 93% in 2025, driven by cost-of-living pressures that make below-market premiums attractive. An emerging evolution is the "ghost portal" — fraudsters now build and sell entire fake insurance verification platforms to other criminals, creating a fraud-as-a-service layer within the insurance ecosystem. City of London Police made significant arrests in May 2025, and the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) designated February 2026 as a ghost broking intensification month. UK fraud losses topped GBP 1 billion in 2024, with ghost broking contributing a material share of motor insurance fraud.
**Distinction from TP-0056**: TP-0056 covers claims fraud (filing false or inflated claims against legitimate policies). TP-0074 covers the upstream fraud of selling fake or unauthorized policies themselves, where the victim believes they have legitimate coverage but does not.

item.title: [TP-0075] Friendly Fraud & Chargeback Abuse
item.description:
Friendly fraud — where legitimate cardholders dispute genuine transactions to obtain refunds while retaining goods or services — has become the single largest fraud category in payment networks, representing 36% of all fraud and projected to reach 337 million chargebacks costing USD 15.3 billion in the US by 2026. Unlike third-party fraud, the identity is real and the transaction is legitimate, making detection fundamentally different. Chargeback abuse surged 233% between Q1 and Q3 2025, with 84% of consumers finding chargebacks simpler than contacting the merchant. The economic multiplier is severe: merchants lose USD 4.61 for every USD 1.00 of friendly fraud. Visa's VAMP (Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program) launched April 2025 to impose stricter thresholds on merchants and acquirers. Underground "refund hack" tutorials proliferate on forums and social platforms, teaching consumers systematic chargeback abuse techniques.
**Distinction from TP-0031**: TP-0031 covers Refund-as-a-Service (RaaS) — organized refund fraud where third-party services file refunds on behalf of consumers against merchants. TP-0075 covers first-party chargeback abuse where the cardholder directly files disputes through the payment network, bypassing the merchant entirely.
**Distinction from TP-0016**: TP-0016 covers first-party bust-out fraud (synthetic or real identity credit abuse). TP-0075 covers dispute-level abuse of the chargeback mechanism against individual transactions, not credit line bust-outs.

item.title: [TP-0076] Affiliate Network Fraud & Invalid Traffic
item.description:
Affiliate network fraud encompasses a range of techniques where fraudulent affiliates generate fake clicks, impressions, leads, or conversions to earn illegitimate commissions from advertiser programs. Global ad fraud is projected to reach USD 71 billion in 2025 (Juniper Research). Cookie stuffing accounts for approximately 60% of affiliate fraud cases, while bot networks generate 40% of all click fraud. AI-powered bots are increasingly mimicking genuine user behavior — generating realistic mouse movements, scroll patterns, and session durations — making detection significantly harder. Approximately 25% of leads generated through affiliate programs are fake, wasting advertiser spend and corrupting marketing analytics. Click injection and postback manipulation represent emerging techniques that exploit mobile attribution windows and server-side tracking vulnerabilities respectively.
**Relationship to TP-0042 (TDS)**: Traffic Distribution Systems documented in TP-0042 provide infrastructure that affiliate fraudsters exploit for traffic manipulation and redirection. TP-0076 covers the affiliate fraud techniques themselves rather than the TDS infrastructure.

item.title: [TP-0077] AI-Generated Insurance Claims Fraud
item.description:
Generative AI is transforming insurance claims fraud by enabling fraudsters to create highly convincing fabricated or altered evidence — including deepfake vehicle damage photos, forged medical records, synthetic invoices, and AI-generated supporting documentation. An estimated 25-30% of insurance claims now involve some form of GenAI-altered content, ranging from minor photo manipulation to entirely fabricated damage scenarios. Deepfake vehicle damage photos represent a particularly acute threat, with AI-generated images of vehicle damage that can bypass visual inspection by claims adjusters. The 2025 US Healthcare Fraud Takedown (324 defendants, USD 14.6 billion in alleged fraud) demonstrated the scale of organized claims fraud that AI tools can amplify. The insurance fraud detection market is growing from USD 7.5 billion to USD 9.13 billion, reflecting industry investment in countermeasures. Academic research (Debener et al., 2023) demonstrates that XGBoost and isolation forest algorithms are complementary approaches for detecting anomalous claims patterns.
**Distinction from TP-0056**: TP-0056 covers traditional claims fraud (exaggerated, staged, or fabricated claims using conventional methods). TP-0077 specifically covers the use of generative AI tools to create or alter claims evidence, which requires different detection techniques focused on digital forensics and AI artifact analysis rather than claims pattern analytics alone.
**Distinction from TP-0029/TP-0018**: TP-0029 covers AI-generated synthetic identities and TP-0018 covers deepfake document fraud broadly. TP-0077 focuses on the specific application of these techniques within the insurance claims process, where the claims workflow creates unique detection opportunities.

item.title: [TP-0078] Stablecoin Laundering via Centralized Exchange Hot Wallet Pipelines
item.description:
Criminal conglomerates are operating industrialized cryptocurrency laundering services that process hundreds of millions of dollars through centralized exchange (CEX) hot wallet pipelines. Unlike the narco-terror Ponzi convergence model documented in TP-0055, this threat path describes a distinct operational model: a criminal organization that builds and operates a full-service laundering infrastructure — issuing its own stablecoin, running its own exchange, and routing proceeds through major centralized exchanges via traceable deposit-to-hot-wallet sweep patterns.
The Huione Group, a Cambodian financial conglomerate designated by FinCEN as a primary money laundering concern in May 2025, is the paradigm case. ICIJ's year-long "Coin Laundry" investigation documented at least $408 million flowing from Huione-controlled TRON addresses to Binance and at least $226 million to OKX over approximately one year (July 2024 to July 2025). The group operated Huione Pay (a cryptocurrency exchange) and issued its own stablecoin (USDH) deployed across four major blockchains: Ethereum, TRON, Binance Smart Chain, and Solana. TRON/USDT was identified as the dominant rail for Southeast Asian fraud compound money laundering due to speed and low transaction fees.
Critically, neither Binance nor OKX demonstrably curtailed their transaction volume with Huione following their own DOJ plea agreements (Binance: November 2023; OKX: February 2025), indicating that plea-deal compliance commitments did not immediately translate into effective flow interdiction.
The convergence of this laundering infrastructure with offshore shell company opacity (see DL-0198) and unlicensed crypto-to-cash desk operations (see DL-0197) creates a complete end-to-end pipeline from illicit proceeds to usable physical currency.
**Key Distinction from TP-0055**: TP-0055 covers narco-terror organizations using crypto Ponzi schemes to launder drug/extortion proceeds — the criminal actors *using* crypto as a laundering tool. TP-0078 covers the *industrialized laundering service provider* model — a criminal conglomerate offering laundering-as-a-service at scale via its own stablecoin and exchange infrastructure, serving multiple criminal actor types including SE Asian scam compounds.
**Key Distinction from TP-0049**: TP-0049 covers cryptocurrency laundering infrastructure broadly. TP-0078 provides the specific operational pattern of the stablecoin-to-CEX hot wallet pipeline, including the 2-hop attribution methodology and Proof-of-Reserves cross-referencing technique.

item.title: [TP-0079] Cheap gTLD and PaaS Subdomain Abuse for Fraud Infrastructure at Scale
item.description:
Phishing infrastructure has undergone a structural shift toward cheap new generic top-level domains (gTLDs) and free Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) subdomains as the dominant delivery mechanism for credential harvesting, brand impersonation, and fraud-enabling infrastructure at global scale. Interisle Consulting Group's Phishing Landscape 2025 report, covering May 2024 through April 2025, documented approximately 2 million phishing attacks worldwide across more than 1.5 million unique domains — with 77% of phishing domains identified as maliciously registered (a 36% year-over-year increase).
The defining finding is the dramatic asymmetry between new gTLD market share and phishing concentration: new gTLDs hold only 11% of the global domain market but accounted for 51% of all phishing domains during the reporting period. This represents a significant escalation from 21% in 2021, indicating that threat actors have systematically migrated to new gTLDs as their preferred registration namespace. The economic driver is clear: 18 new gTLDs offered registrations under $2, and sub-$2 pricing correlates directly with the highest phishing abuse scores.
Simultaneously, PaaS subdomain abuse has emerged as a parallel infrastructure channel. Cloudflare pages.dev saw a 157% increase in phishing attacks (43,800 attacks), Webflow's webflow.io surged 980% (33,400 attacks), Vercel's vercel.app grew 279% (21,400 attacks), and GitBook's gitbook.io appeared as a new vector with 22,000 attacks. These platforms provide free hosting with legitimate SSL certificates and trusted domain reputations, enabling phishers to bypass email security filters and browser warnings.
A specific campaign — the "Unpaid Toll Scam" — illustrates the convergence of these techniques: 37,000 domains were registered via Dominet (HK) registrar across the .XIN and .TOP TLDs, operated by the Chinese PhaaS provider XinXin/LUCID, and hosted on Tencent (AS132203), Alibaba (AS45102), and Cloudflare (AS13335) infrastructure. IDN homograph attacks further compound the threat, with 2,655 domains targeting cryptocurrency brands through internationalized domain name spoofing (e.g., xn--btpay-b4a.com rendering as bitpay.com).
Cloudflare AS13335 has been the number one hosting network for phishing attacks for four consecutive years, with 540,000 attacks during the reporting period, largely because its reverse proxy architecture obscures the true hosting location of phishing pages from investigators and automated takedown systems.

item.title: [TP-0080] Stablecoin Freeze-Evasion via Wrapped Tokens, Decentralized Stablecoins, and Cross-Chain Bridges
item.description:
State-sponsored threat actors and transnational criminal organizations have developed a systematic methodology to evade stablecoin issuer freeze capabilities by converting centrally issued stablecoins (USDT, USDC) into decentralized alternatives (DAI, sDAI, LUSD, RAI) and wrapped token variants that decouple the original issuer's administrative controls. This threat path exploits a fundamental architectural gap: when a centrally issued stablecoin is "wrapped" through a bridge protocol or swapped for a decentralized stablecoin, the issuer's freeze function — the primary compliance enforcement mechanism — becomes inoperable against the resulting tokens.
The FATF Targeted Report on Stablecoins and Unhosted Wallets (March 2026) quantifies the scale: stablecoins accounted for 84% of the $154 billion in illicit virtual asset transaction volume observed in 2025 (Chainalysis data). This dominance reflects stablecoins' utility as a stable-value transfer mechanism for illicit actors who cannot tolerate the price volatility of BTC or ETH during multi-stage laundering operations.
Two confirmed nation-state programs demonstrate this threat path at operational scale. The IRGC shifted procurement financing from USDT to DAI following mid-2025 Tether freeze actions, using decentralized stablecoins to purchase drone components and weapons systems through front companies. Billions in IRGC-associated addresses were identified across 2024-2025. Separately, the DPRK's Lazarus Group laundered proceeds from the $1.46 billion Bybit theft (February 2025) through mixers, cross-chain bridges, and 125,000+ Ethereum wallets before converting to USDT on TRON for OTC cash-out — with the 221 General Bureau using USDT for military equipment procurement including munitions-grade copper.
Beyond state actors, drug trafficking organizations are using USDT on TRON and USDC on Ethereum for synthetic drug precursor procurement and settlement. ISIL and Al-Qaeda affiliates have solicited stablecoin donations via encrypted messaging platforms, employing rotating wallet addresses, micro-splitting, and multi-hop transfers to evade tracing.
The convergence of P2P transactions via unhosted wallets (no AML/CFT intermediary), cross-chain bridge fragmentation of transaction trails, and decentralized stablecoin adoption creates a compounding evasion capability that existing compliance frameworks — designed around centralized issuer controls — are structurally unable to address.
**Key Distinction from TP-0078**: TP-0078 documents the industrialized laundering-as-a-service pipeline model (Huione Group, CEX hot wallet sweep patterns). TP-0080 documents the upstream evasion technique: how illicit actors defeat the freeze capability that is supposed to prevent stablecoins from being used in the TP-0078 pipeline in the first place. TP-0080 feeds into TP-0078 — once freeze-evasion is achieved, the resulting funds flow through the CEX off-ramp infrastructure documented in TP-0078.
**Key Distinction from TP-0049**: TP-0049 covers cryptocurrency laundering infrastructure broadly. TP-0080 specifically addresses the exploitation of stablecoin architectural design — the gap between centralized issuance with freeze capabilities and decentralized/wrapped circulation without them — as a deliberate sanctions and law enforcement evasion technique.

item.title: [TP-0081] Vishing-Led Identity Abuse and Hybrid Social Engineering for Financial Fraud
item.description:
Voice phishing (vishing) has emerged as the dominant initial access vector for identity-based intrusions, with adversaries combining real-time phone-based social engineering with technical exploitation chains to achieve account takeover at unprecedented speed. The CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report documents a convergence of vishing, fake CAPTCHA campaigns, help desk impersonation, and GenAI-enabled persona creation that collectively represent a paradigm shift away from malware-centric attack models. 82% of CrowdStrike-observed detections in 2025 were malware-free, relying instead on valid credentials, native tools, and administrative functions.
CHATTY SPIDER exemplifies the operational tempo: in a documented incident against a law firm, the adversary achieved a 4-minute breakout from initial vishing contact to active data exfiltration. Fake CAPTCHA campaigns surged 563% in 2025, with threat actors (BRASH SPIDER, COOKIE SPIDER) tricking victims into executing clipboard-delivered PowerShell payloads. SCATTERED SPIDER continues to social-engineer help desk personnel into performing password resets on SSO and cloud accounts, exploiting hybrid identity infrastructure (Entra ID, AD FS) for lateral movement. Average eCrime breakout time has collapsed to 29 minutes (down 65% from 48 minutes in 2024; fastest observed: 27 seconds), making real-time detection and response essential.
AI-enabled adversary attacks rose 89%, with GenAI used to create convincing voice personas, synthetic identities for fraudulent employment (FAMOUS CHOLLIMA, +109% in fake personas), and multi-day social engineering campaigns (COZY BEAR leveraging instant messaging, email, video conferencing, and OAuth 2.0 device code phishing). Financial services accounted for 11% of interactive intrusion targets, with technology at 23%.
**Distinction from TP-0067**: TP-0067 covers AiTM phishing kit infrastructure and session token hijacking via reverse proxy platforms. TP-0081 focuses on the voice-based and hybrid social engineering attack surface — vishing, help desk manipulation, fake CAPTCHA campaigns, and RMM tool abuse — where the human operator, not a phishing kit, is the primary attack instrument. The two threat paths frequently chain: vishing provides initial access that enables AiTM-style session capture downstream.

item.title: [TP-0082] Gold Courier Scam — Physical Precious Metal Cash-Out
item.description: Gold courier scams represent a novel physical monetization technique where victims — predominantly elderly — are deceived through government impersonation phone calls into converting bank deposits to physical gold, which is then collected by couriers dispatched by the criminal network. The FBI IC3 2025 Annual Report documented 725 complaints with $311.8 million in losses, yielding an extraordinary average loss of approximately $430,000 per victim — among the highest of any IC3 crime category. The physical gold acquisition and courier collection circumvents traditional electronic transaction monitoring, making this a detection blind spot for institutions relying solely on digital payment analytics.

item.title: [TP-0083] Investment Club Scam — Social Media Insider Group Fraud
item.description: Investment club scams exploit social media and messaging platforms to create fraudulent "insider" trading groups that lure victims with fabricated trading success, AI-generated celebrity endorsements, and peer pressure dynamics. The FBI IC3 2025 Annual Report documented approximately 1,600 complaints with $160 million in losses, and PSA250703 (July 3, 2025) specifically warned about investment clubs accessed on social media and messaging applications. Unlike traditional pig butchering (TP-0017) which relies on 1:1 grooming, investment club scams leverage group dynamics — social proof from other "members" (often shills or bots), fake trading screenshots, and the illusion of an exclusive community — to accelerate victim conversion and increase investment amounts.

item.title: [TP-0084] Government Impersonation — Authority-Based Authorized Push Payment Fraud
item.description:
Government impersonation fraud uses the authority of federal and state agencies — IRS, SSA, DOJ, FBI, DEA, and state attorneys general — as a social engineering weapon to compel victims into making authorized push payments. The FBI IC3 2025 Annual Report documented 32,424 complaints with $797.9 million in losses, representing an 87% increase in complaints and 97% increase in losses from 2024. This is fundamentally distinct from government program fraud (TP-0022) which exploits government systems for unauthorized benefit claims. Here, the government is not the victim — it is the impersonated authority used to intimidate and control the actual victim.
The payment channel distribution reveals the scheme's adaptability: Cryptocurrency 40%, Wire Transfer/ACH 21%, Prepaid card/Gift card 15%, Cash 14%, Check/Cashier's Check 10%. Victims aged 60+ are disproportionately targeted, accounting for 8,628 complaints and $413.2 million in losses (52% of total losses).
A notable sub-variant involves scammers impersonating the FBI IC3 itself (PSA250418), exploiting victims' awareness of IC3 as a fraud reporting resource to add credibility to recovery or refund schemes.

item.title: [TP-0085] Crypto ATM/Kiosk Directed Fraud — Physical-to-Digital Monetization Channel
item.description:
Crypto ATM/kiosk fraud is a cross-cutting monetization channel where victims of upstream fraud schemes (tech support, government impersonation, romance, investment) are directed to deposit cash at cryptocurrency ATMs/kiosks, converting physical currency to digital assets that are immediately transferred to attacker-controlled wallets. The FBI IC3 2025 Annual Report documented 13,460 complaints with $389 million in losses — a 58% increase from 2024. The elder demographic is disproportionately impacted: victims aged 60+ accounted for 6,188 complaints (46%) and $257 million in losses (66% of total crypto ATM losses).
This TP is distinct from general cryptocurrency fraud because it focuses specifically on the physical-to-digital conversion point — the crypto ATM itself — as the execution and monetization channel. The crypto ATM serves as the critical chokepoint where detection and intervention are possible before funds become irrecoverable on-chain.

item.title: [DL-0001] Mule Account Velocity Pattern
item.description: Detects rapid inbound transfers from multiple unique senders followed by immediate outbound movement, typical of money mule activity. This rule is a shared component applicable to TP-0001, TP-0002, TP-0011, and TP-0022.

item.title: [DL-0002] Infostealer Credential Dump Velocity
item.description: Detects rapid credential dump patterns where many unique credentials are harvested from a single host in a short timeframe. Infostealers such as RedLine, Lumma, and Vidar typically exfiltrate dozens to hundreds of stored credentials within seconds of execution, producing a burst of credential-access events from one endpoint.

item.title: [DL-0003] Session Cookie Exfiltration Pattern
item.description: Detects session token and cookie theft patterns in log data indicative of infostealer activity. Stealers like Lumma and Raccoon target browser cookie stores to extract active session tokens, enabling session hijacking without requiring credentials. This rule monitors for suspicious access to cookie databases and exfiltration of session-bearing data.

item.title: [DL-0004] Browser Credential Store Access
item.description: Detects unusual access to browser credential stores (Login Data, logins.json, key3.db/key4.db) by non-browser processes. Infostealers such as RedLine and Vidar systematically read these SQLite databases to extract saved usernames and passwords for banking portals and other financial services.

item.title: [DL-0005] Stealer C2 Beacon Pattern
item.description: Detects command-and-control callback patterns typical of Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) stealers. RedLine, Lumma, and StealC use distinctive C2 communication patterns including HTTP POST requests with base64-encoded payloads to newly registered domains, often on non-standard ports or with characteristic URI patterns.

item.title: [DL-0006] Credential Testing After Dump
item.description: Detects rapid credential validation attempts occurring shortly after a credential dump event. After infostealers exfiltrate harvested credentials, threat actors typically run automated validation to identify which stolen credentials are still active, producing a burst of login attempts across multiple banking portals from the attacker's infrastructure.

item.title: [DL-0007] Infostealer Exfiltration Archive Creation
item.description: Detects creation of archive files containing credential-related file patterns consistent with infostealer packaging behavior. Stealers like RedLine and Vidar collect credentials, cookies, autofill data, and crypto wallet files into a ZIP or RAR archive before exfiltrating them to the C2 server.

item.title: [DL-0008] Multiple Account Access from Single Source
item.description: Detects multiple distinct banking accounts being accessed from a single device or IP address within a short timeframe. This pattern is consistent with an attacker using stolen credentials from an infostealer dump to sequentially access compromised accounts for reconnaissance or initial positioning before fraudulent transactions.

item.title: [DL-0009] Stolen Session Token Replay
item.description: Detects session token replay from a different geographic location or device than the original authenticating session. When infostealers exfiltrate active session cookies, attackers import them into antidetect browsers to hijack authenticated sessions without triggering login-based detections. This rule correlates session token usage across differing geolocations and device fingerprints.

item.title: [DL-0010] Autofill Data Harvesting
item.description: Detects form autofill data extraction patterns consistent with infostealer behavior. Stealers like RedLine and Raccoon target browser autofill databases (Web Data, formhistory.sqlite) to harvest stored PII including names, addresses, phone numbers, and payment card details that facilitate downstream fraud.

item.title: [DL-0011] Crypto Wallet Seed Phrase Exfiltration
item.description: Detects wallet seed phrase and private key extraction attempts targeting cryptocurrency wallets. Infostealers such as RedLine, Vidar, and StealC include dedicated modules that search for wallet.dat files, seed phrase backups, and keystore directories for MetaMask, Exodus, Electrum, and other popular wallets to enable cryptocurrency theft.

item.title: [DL-0012] Login Velocity Anomaly
item.description: Detects abnormal login attempt velocity from a single source IP or subnet, indicative of automated credential stuffing tools. Legitimate users produce low single-digit login attempts per minute; credential stuffing tools generate dozens to hundreds, often targeting the authentication API directly rather than the web login form.

item.title: [DL-0013] Geographic Impossibility Login
item.description: Detects login attempts from geographically impossible locations within a short timeframe. When a user authenticates from one country and a second authentication occurs from a distant country within a window that makes physical travel impossible, it strongly indicates credential compromise and concurrent use by an attacker.

item.title: [DL-0014] Device Fingerprint Anomaly
item.description: Detects a known device fingerprint presenting with changed underlying characteristics such as OS version, screen resolution, timezone, or installed fonts. Attackers using antidetect browsers (Multilogin, GoLogin, Dolphin Anty) import stolen device fingerprints but often have mismatches in lower-level hardware attributes that this rule correlates.

item.title: [DL-0015] Combo List Iteration Pattern
item.description: Detects sequential username patterns typical of combo list iteration during credential stuffing attacks. Attackers feed sorted credential lists into stuffing tools, producing login attempts where usernames appear in alphabetical or near-alphabetical order with minimal timing variation between attempts, a pattern never seen in organic user behavior.

item.title: [DL-0016] Distributed Credential Stuffing
item.description: Detects low-and-slow distributed credential stuffing attacks spread across multiple source IPs to evade per-IP rate limiting. Advanced attackers use residential proxy networks and botnets to distribute attempts, making each source IP appear benign while the aggregate attack targets many accounts. This rule aggregates failed login patterns across source IPs sharing common characteristics.

item.title: [DL-0017] Residential Proxy Login Attempt
item.description: Detects login attempts originating from known residential proxy networks. Credential stuffing actors increasingly route attacks through residential proxies (Luminati/Bright Data, Oxylabs, SmartProxy) to appear as legitimate home users and bypass IP-reputation blocklists. This rule correlates source IPs against residential proxy threat intelligence feeds.

item.title: [DL-0018] Credential Spray Single Password
item.description: Detects password spraying attacks where a single password (or small set of passwords) is tested across many accounts. Unlike traditional credential stuffing which uses unique username-password pairs, password spraying tries common or recently breached passwords against a large account population to avoid per-account lockout thresholds.

item.title: [DL-0019] Beneficiary Change Velocity Anomaly
item.description: Detects multiple beneficiary additions or modifications on a single account within a short time window. Rapid beneficiary changes are a strong pre-cursor to payment diversion fraud, where an attacker positions new destination accounts before initiating unauthorized wires.

item.title: [DL-0020] Rapid Contact Information Change
item.description: Detects when email, phone number, and mailing address are all changed on an account within a short window. A full contact information swap is a hallmark of account takeover where the attacker locks out the legitimate owner before executing fraud.

item.title: [DL-0021] MFA Method Switch Before High-Value Transaction
item.description: Detects when an account's multi-factor authentication method is changed (e.g., from hardware token to SMS or email OTP) shortly before a high-value wire or ACH transaction is initiated. Attackers downgrade MFA to a method they control prior to executing fraud.

item.title: [DL-0022] Dormant Account Reactivation
item.description: Detects accounts with no transactional activity for 90 or more days that suddenly initiate financial transactions. Dormant accounts are frequently targeted by attackers because they are less likely to be monitored and credential compromise may go unnoticed.

item.title: [DL-0023] Alert Threshold Modification
item.description: Detects when a user modifies their own transaction alert thresholds or disables notifications via online banking or mobile app. Attackers raise alert thresholds or suppress notifications to prevent the legitimate account holder from being alerted to unauthorized transactions.

item.title: [DL-0024] Wire Beneficiary Name Mismatch
item.description: Detects when the wire beneficiary name provided by the originator does not match the account holder name at the receiving institution. Name mismatches on wire transfers are a strong indicator of payment diversion fraud where funds are redirected to accounts controlled by the attacker.

item.title: [DL-0025] Power of Attorney or Authorized Signer Change
item.description: Detects changes to power of attorney designations or authorized signers on commercial and business accounts. Fraudsters may socially engineer or forge POA documents to gain control of business accounts, enabling them to initiate high-value transactions.

item.title: [DL-0026] Account Type Conversion Anomaly
item.description: Detects suspicious account type conversions such as savings-to-checking or personal-to-business. These conversions can unlock higher transaction limits, wire capabilities, or ACH origination, which attackers exploit to move larger amounts after taking over a limited account.

item.title: [DL-0027] First-Time International Wire to New Country
item.description: Detects international wire transfers sent to a country that has no prior transaction history for the originating account. First-time international wires, especially to high-risk corridors, are a key indicator of business email compromise and payment diversion schemes.

item.title: [DL-0028] Transaction Amount Clustering Near Reporting Threshold
item.description: Detects transactions that cluster just below regulatory reporting thresholds ($3,000 for international transfers, $10,000 for CTR filing). Structuring transactions to evade reporting requirements is itself a federal offense and a strong indicator of money laundering or fraud monetization.

item.title: [DL-0029] Split Transfer Chain Detection
item.description: Detects when a large inbound amount is split into multiple smaller outbound transfers to different beneficiaries in sequence. This layering technique is used to obscure the origin and destination of fraudulently obtained funds.

item.title: [DL-0030] After-Hours Wire Transfer Initiation
item.description: Detects wire transfers initiated outside the account's established normal business hours. Attackers often execute unauthorized wires during evenings, weekends, or holidays when fraud detection staff and account holders are less likely to notice.

item.title: [DL-0031] Rapid Outbound Wire After Large Inbound
item.description: Detects a large outbound wire or ACH transfer initiated within hours of receiving a large inbound deposit. This pass-through pattern is characteristic of compromised accounts being used as intermediary conduits in fraud or money laundering schemes.

item.title: [DL-0032] Beneficiary Country Mismatch with Business Profile
item.description: Detects wire transfers to countries where the account holder has no established business relationship or prior transaction history. Combined with other indicators, this can reveal business email compromise where payment instructions are altered to redirect funds to attacker-controlled accounts in foreign jurisdictions.

item.title: [DL-0033] Round-Dollar Wire Amount Pattern
item.description: Detects unusual patterns of wire transfers in round dollar amounts (e.g., $5,000, $10,000, $25,000). While individual round-amount wires are common, a pattern of multiple round-amount wires is atypical for legitimate business payments and may indicate structured or test transactions by fraudsters.

item.title: [DL-0034] ACH Return Rate Anomaly
item.description: Detects ACH originators with an elevated return or reversal rate exceeding normal thresholds. High ACH return rates (especially R10 unauthorized, R29 corporate not authorized) may indicate the account is being used to initiate unauthorized debits against victim accounts.

item.title: [DL-0035] Wire to FATF High-Risk Jurisdiction
item.description: Detects wire transfers to jurisdictions on the FATF high-risk or increased monitoring lists. While not inherently fraudulent, wires to these jurisdictions combined with other risk factors (new beneficiary, unusual amount, after-hours) significantly elevate the risk of money laundering or fraud monetization.

item.title: [DL-0036] Payment Instruction Velocity Spike
item.description: Detects when multiple payment instructions (wires, ACH batches, or internal transfers) are submitted in rapid succession from a single account or user session. High-velocity payment submissions suggest automated or scripted fraud execution, often seen after credential compromise.

item.title: [DL-0037] Mule Rapid ATM Withdrawal After Inbound Transfer
item.description: Detects cash withdrawals at ATMs occurring shortly after an inbound wire or ACH transfer. Money mules frequently convert electronically received fraud proceeds to cash as quickly as possible to prevent recovery, often hitting daily ATM limits across multiple machines.

item.title: [DL-0038] Account Age vs Transaction Volume Mismatch
item.description: Detects accounts less than 90 days old that exhibit transaction volumes exceeding the typical profile for mature accounts. Newly opened accounts with abnormally high volume are a primary indicator of purpose-built mule accounts created specifically to funnel illicit funds.

item.title: [DL-0039] Multi-Bank Funnel Pattern
item.description: Detects accounts receiving funds from multiple external financial institutions that are then consolidated and sent outbound to a single destination. This funnel pattern is a hallmark of money mule operations where proceeds from multiple fraud victims are aggregated before being laundered.

item.title: [DL-0040] Crypto Off-Ramp After Wire or ACH Receipt
item.description: Detects a pattern where an account receives a wire or ACH credit and then promptly initiates a transfer to a known cryptocurrency exchange or digital asset platform. Converting fraud proceeds to cryptocurrency provides near-irreversible laundering, making this a critical monetization indicator.

item.title: [DL-0041] Peer-to-Peer Transfer Chain (Smurfing Pattern)
item.description: Detects chains of peer-to-peer transfers across multiple accounts where funds move through a sequence of intermediary accounts (A to B to C to D). This smurfing pattern is used to layer fraud proceeds through multiple hops, making tracing difficult.

item.title: [DL-0042] Mule Recruitment Test Deposit Pattern
item.description: Detects accounts receiving multiple small "test" deposits from many distinct external sources. Mule recruiters validate new mule accounts by sending micro-deposits from various fraud proceeds before routing larger amounts. The pattern of many small inbound transfers from unrelated senders is highly anomalous for personal accounts.

item.title: [DL-0043] Rapid Fund Layering Through Shell Accounts
item.description: Detects rapid fund movement through multiple accounts with minimal retention time, indicative of layering through shell or pass-through accounts. Funds transit through each account within hours with near-zero balance retention, suggesting the accounts exist solely to obscure the money trail.

item.title: [DL-0044] Carrier Change Authentication Correlation
item.description: Detects a carrier or SIM change event immediately followed by an authentication attempt on a banking platform. SIM swap attacks involve social engineering or insider compromise at a mobile carrier to port the victim's phone number to an attacker-controlled SIM, after which the attacker uses SMS-based MFA to access accounts. The tight temporal correlation between carrier change and login is the key indicator.

item.title: [DL-0045] New Device High-Value Transaction
item.description: Detects a high-value financial transaction initiated from a new or previously unknown device shortly after initial authentication. Attackers who have compromised credentials and bypassed MFA via SIM swap typically move quickly to execute high-value transfers from a device with no prior history on the account, exploiting the narrow window before the victim notices.

item.title: [DL-0046] MFA Push Bombing
item.description: Detects rapid repeated MFA push notifications sent to the same user, a technique known as MFA fatigue or push bombing. Attackers who have obtained valid credentials bombard the victim with push authentication requests, hoping the user will approve one out of frustration or confusion, thereby granting the attacker access.

item.title: [DL-0047] SIM Swap Indicator Chain
item.description: Detects the full SIM swap attack chain: phone number change followed by password reset followed by high-value account action in rapid sequence. This multi-stage correlation captures the complete attack lifecycle where the attacker first takes over the phone number, then uses it to reset the account password via SMS OTP, and finally executes a high-value transfer or account modification.

item.title: [DL-0048] VoIP Number MFA Enrollment
item.description: Detects MFA enrollment using VoIP or virtual phone numbers instead of legitimate mobile carrier numbers. Attackers who have compromised an account often enroll a disposable VoIP number (Google Voice, TextNow, Twilio) as the MFA phone to maintain persistent access and intercept future OTP codes without relying on SIM swap persistence.

item.title: [DL-0049] MFA Method Downgrade
item.description: Detects when an account's MFA method is changed from a strong phishing-resistant factor (FIDO2/WebAuthn, hardware token, authenticator app) to a weaker method (SMS OTP, voice call). Attackers who compromise account credentials may downgrade the MFA method to one they can intercept via SIM swap or SS7 exploitation, enabling persistent account takeover.

item.title: [DL-0050] Voice Biometric Confidence Score Anomaly for Known Caller
item.description: Detects when a voice biometric verification score for a previously enrolled caller falls below an acceptable confidence threshold, which may indicate a deepfake or voice-clone attempt impersonating a legitimate customer. Legitimate callers typically produce scores above 85; scores between 40-70 with a previously stable voiceprint warrant investigation.

item.title: [DL-0051] Callback Number Mismatch for Claimed Institution
item.description: Detects when an inbound caller claims to represent a specific financial institution or internal department, but the originating ANI or callback number does not match the institution's known directory of outbound numbers. This is a common indicator of vishing and social engineering, especially when combined with voice-clone technology to impersonate bank officials.

item.title: [DL-0052] Audio Compression Artifacts Indicative of AI-Generated Speech
item.description: Detects audio streams exhibiting compression artifacts, spectral anomalies, or frequency-band irregularities characteristic of AI-generated or text-to-speech synthesis engines. These include unnaturally uniform pitch contours, missing micro-pauses, absence of breath sounds, and codec artifacts from re-encoding through real-time deepfake pipelines.

item.title: [DL-0053] Deepfake Anomalies in Video KYC Session
item.description: Detects anomalies during video KYC (Know Your Customer) sessions that may indicate the use of deepfake technology. Indicators include irregular frame rates suggesting real-time face-swapping, inconsistent lighting between face and background, lip-sync desynchronization, unnatural eye-blink patterns, and face-boundary artifacts.

item.title: [DL-0054] AI-Generated Document Detection in Verification
item.description: Detects indicators of AI-generated or synthetically created identity documents submitted during verification workflows. Flags include metadata anomalies (missing EXIF data, uniform noise patterns), font rendering inconsistencies, micro-printing irregularities, and GAN-generated portrait artifacts such as asymmetric earrings or irregular hair boundaries.

item.title: [DL-0055] Real-Time Payment to New Payee After Credential or Contact Change
item.description: Detects when a real-time or instant payment (Zelle, FedNow, RTP) is initiated to a previously unseen payee within 24 hours of a credential change (password reset, MFA re-enrollment) or contact information update (email, phone, address). This pattern is strongly associated with account takeover followed by immediate monetization via authorized push payment.

item.title: [DL-0056] Instant Payment Velocity Spike Above 30-Day Baseline
item.description: Detects a sudden spike in instant payment frequency that significantly exceeds the account's established 30-day baseline. A spike is defined as the current day's instant payment count exceeding 3 standard deviations above the rolling 30-day mean, indicating potential account compromise or mule activity where the account is being drained rapidly.

item.title: [DL-0057] Cross-Platform Deposit and Withdrawal Chain
item.description: Detects a pattern where funds are received via one payment rail (e.g., ACH, wire) and then immediately sent out via a different payment rail (e.g., Zelle, FedNow) within a short window. This cross-rail chaining is a common layering technique used to obscure the origin of funds and complicate tracing, often associated with money mule operations and authorized push payment fraud monetization.

item.title: [DL-0058] Repeated A2A Payments at Maximum Per-Transaction Limit
item.description: Detects multiple account-to-account payments where each transaction is at or near the maximum per-transaction limit (e.g., $2,500 for Zelle, $500,000 for FedNow). Fraudsters often structure payments at the exact limit to maximize extraction speed while avoiding aggregate-amount alerts, a behavior rarely seen in legitimate consumer transactions.

item.title: [DL-0059] New Account Sending Multiple Instant Payments
item.description: Detects accounts less than 30 days old that initiate multiple instant payments within a short time window. Newly opened accounts used for rapid instant-payment disbursement are a strong indicator of synthetic identity fraud or mule accounts created specifically for the monetization phase of a fraud scheme.

item.title: [DL-0060] Zelle Recipient Enumeration via Multiple Failed Lookups
item.description: Detects multiple failed Zelle recipient lookups from a single account or session, which may indicate enumeration activity. Attackers probe email addresses and phone numbers to identify which are registered with Zelle before launching targeted social engineering or authorized push payment attacks against confirmed users.

item.title: [DL-0061] Real-Time Payment Followed by Immediate Refund or Return Request
item.description: Detects a pattern where a real-time payment (RTP or FedNow) is sent and then an immediate refund, return, or Request for Return of Funds (RROF) is submitted within a short window. This pattern may indicate a double-dip fraud scheme where the sender initiates an irrevocable payment, then exploits the refund process to recover funds while the recipient also retains them.

item.title: [DL-0062] Fake Tracking ID (FTID) Refund Fraud Indicators
item.description: Detects indicators of fake tracking ID (FTID) refund fraud, where a customer claims a package was not received or returned by providing a manipulated or fabricated tracking number. Indicators include tracking numbers that show delivery to the carrier facility but not to the customer address, tracking IDs associated with lightweight packages inconsistent with the order, or reuse of known FTID patterns across multiple refund claims.

item.title: [DL-0063] Abnormally High Refund Rate Per Customer Account
item.description: Detects customer accounts with an abnormally high refund-to-order ratio over a rolling window. Accounts exceeding a refund rate of 40% across 10 or more orders within 90 days are flagged as potential refund abusers or participants in refunding-as-a-service (RaaS) schemes, where professional refunders exploit return policies systematically.

item.title: [DL-0064] Triangulation Fraud Shipping Pattern Detection
item.description: Detects orders where the shipping address differs from the billing address and matches known drop-ship or reshipping patterns associated with triangulation fraud. In triangulation fraud, a fraudster lists goods on a marketplace, collects payment from a victim buyer, then purchases the item from a legitimate retailer using stolen payment credentials, shipping directly to the victim. Indicators include shipping to known drop addresses, freight forwarders, or addresses seen across multiple unrelated accounts.

item.title: [DL-0065] Return Without Receipt Clustering by Customer or Region
item.description: Detects clusters of product returns submitted without receipts or order references from the same customer identity or geographic region. Organized return fraud rings often exploit no-receipt return policies by using stolen merchandise or purchasing items specifically for return, concentrating activity across nearby store locations or using multiple accounts linked to the same region.

item.title: [DL-0066] High-Value Item Not Received Claims Exceeding Threshold
item.description: Detects "item not received" (INR) claims filed on high-value orders that exceed a configurable dollar threshold. High-value INR claims are a primary vector for refund fraud, particularly when the delivery confirmation shows successful delivery. Repeated INR claims on expensive items from the same account or device fingerprint are strong indicators of first-party fraud or professional refunding services.

item.title: [DL-0067] Excessive Promotional Code or Coupon Abuse from Related Accounts
item.description: Detects excessive use of promotional codes, referral bonuses, or coupon offers from accounts that share common attributes such as device fingerprint, IP address, payment method, or shipping address. This pattern indicates promo abuse rings that create multiple accounts to exploit new-customer or referral promotions repeatedly, often using synthetic or stolen identities.

item.title: [DL-0068] DPRK IT Worker Resume Geographic Mismatch
item.description: Detects job applicants whose resume combines a U.S. residential address with education credentials from non-North American institutions (Singapore, Japan, Hong Kong, China, South Korea). This pattern is a key DPRK IT worker indicator documented by FBI IC3 and DOJ enforcement actions. Legitimate applicants with this profile exist, but the combination with thin credit files or recently created LinkedIn profiles significantly elevates risk.

item.title: [DL-0069] VPN/Proxy Login Anomaly — Astrill or Residential Proxy
item.description: Detects corporate VPN authentication events originating from known Astrill VPN infrastructure, residential proxy services, or connection patterns indicating VPN-over-VPN layering. DPRK IT workers route connections through Astrill VPN to U.S.-based proxy laptops before connecting to corporate infrastructure, creating a characteristic multi-hop pattern with elevated latency and IP reputation indicators.

item.title: [DL-0070] Multi-Operator Behavioral Shift — Timezone and Communication Anomaly
item.description: Detects behavioral patterns suggesting multiple operators are sharing a single employee identity. Indicators include login activity spanning incompatible timezones within a single day, significant shifts in communication style or vocabulary between time windows, and device fingerprint changes that correlate with timezone transitions. DPRK IT workers often operate in shifts from different locations using the same stolen identity.

item.title: [DL-0071] Bulk Code Repository Clone by New Employee
item.description: Detects a new employee (within first 14 days of onboarding) cloning or downloading multiple code repositories, especially repositories outside their assigned team or project scope. DPRK IT workers frequently begin exfiltrating source code within hours of gaining access, cloning entire organizational repositories to personal GitHub accounts or external cloud storage.

item.title: [DL-0072] Credential Store Access Anomaly During Onboarding
item.description: Detects new employees accessing browser credential stores, password managers, API key management systems, or SSO session token stores at rates significantly above peer baselines during the first 14 days of employment. DPRK IT workers harvest credentials, session cookies, and API keys early in their tenure for exfiltration to DPRK cyber units and as leverage for post-termination extortion.

item.title: [DL-0073] Salary Direct Deposit Rapid Cryptocurrency Conversion
item.description: Detects patterns where salary direct deposit payments are rapidly converted to cryptocurrency (USDT, USDC, BTC) within 48 hours of deposit, particularly when the receiving account was recently opened or when multiple employee accounts show the same conversion pattern through the same exchange or payment processor. DPRK IT workers convert salary to cryptocurrency for transfer to regime-controlled wallets, often using daily conversion limits to avoid AML alerts.

item.title: [DL-0074] Post-Termination Data Extortion Indicator
item.description: Detects indicators of post-termination data extortion, where a recently terminated or resigned employee communicates ransom demands referencing specific internal proprietary code, documents, or trade secrets. DPRK IT workers have escalated to this tactic since mid-2024, threatening to publish exfiltrated source code on public repositories or sell proprietary data unless payment is made. Indicators include communication from personal channels containing references to internal systems, and the appearance of company code on public GitHub repositories created by former employee-linked accounts.

item.title: [DL-0075] E-Skimmer Script Injection on Payment Pages
item.description: Detects unauthorized JavaScript injection on e-commerce payment pages by identifying Content Security Policy violations, unexpected external script loads from newly registered domains, and unauthorized Google Tag Manager container modifications. Magecart-style e-skimmer operators inject malicious scripts through CMS exploitation, compromised third-party libraries, or GTM container abuse. The "Sniffer by Fleras" MaaS platform accounts for 26% of all infections, and GTM container abuse has become a primary delivery vector due to GTM's trusted status in most CSP configurations. PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 6.4.3 mandates automated script integrity monitoring on payment pages, making this detection a compliance requirement as well as a security control.

item.title: [DL-0076] Blockchain C2 and WebSocket Exfiltration from Payment Pages
item.description: Detects payment page scripts making calls to blockchain RPC endpoints or establishing WebSocket connections to unknown servers, indicating potential e-skimmer data exfiltration via blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure. Advanced Magecart variants observed in 2025 use a loader script on the compromised site that queries a blockchain smart contract (Ethereum, BNB Chain) to retrieve the address of a second-stage payload server, then establishes a WebSocket connection for both payload delivery and data exfiltration. This technique provides censorship-resistant C2 that cannot be disrupted through conventional domain seizure or hosting provider takedown. Detection focuses on identifying JSON-RPC calls to blockchain node endpoints (Infura, Alchemy, direct nodes) and WebSocket connections to non-payment-related servers originating from payment page context.

item.title: [DL-0077] Unauthorized Checkout Page DOM Modification
item.description: Detects modifications to checkout page DOM elements — including payment form fields, submit buttons, and iframe injections — that occur outside authorized deployment windows or without corresponding change management records. E-skimmer operators manipulate checkout page DOM to inject fake payment form overlays, intercept form submission events, or create invisible iframes that mirror payment forms to capture card data. Legitimate checkout page modifications should only occur during scheduled deployment windows and should be tracked in version control and change management systems. Any DOM mutation on payment form elements that does not correlate with an authorized release is a high-confidence indicator of e-skimmer injection. This rule supports PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 6.4.3 for script and content integrity monitoring on payment pages.

item.title: [DL-0078] Scam Merchant High-Velocity Transaction Pattern
item.description: Detects merchant accounts exhibiting high initial transaction velocity, elevated chargeback ratios, and short account age — a pattern consistent with purchase scam merchant operations. Recorded Future identified 3,600+ scam merchant accounts in 2025, a 2.5x increase from 2024, operating across 40+ countries and 230+ acquirers. Scam merchants typically process high transaction volumes within their first 30-90 days to extract maximum revenue before chargeback volume triggers acquirer intervention and account termination. Normal new merchant ramp-up is fewer than 50 transactions per day in the first 30 days, ramping to 200+ by day 90. Scam merchants frequently exceed 200 transactions per day within the first two weeks, combined with chargeback rates exceeding 1.5% within 60 days of account opening. This rule also flags merchants with account ages under 90 days that have already accumulated chargeback ratios above scheme monitoring thresholds.

item.title: [DL-0079] Subscription Trap Billing Pattern Detection
item.description: Detects recurring billing patterns characteristic of subscription trap scam merchants, where initial low-value trial charges are followed by significantly higher recurring charges to merchants with elevated dispute rates. Purchase scam operators enroll victims in subscription billing through obscured terms buried in checkout flows — initial charges are typically under $10 (trial pricing) while subsequent recurring charges escalate to $50-$200+ per cycle. Recorded Future identified this pattern across scam merchant networks in 2025, with some operations adding a secondary "transaction recovery service" charge in H2 2025. Detection focuses on merchants where the ratio of maximum to minimum charge amount exceeds 5:1, recurring billing constitutes more than 30% of transactions, initial charges are below $10, and the merchant has an elevated dispute rate relative to its age and category. Normal subscription merchants show a recurring billing enrollment rate of 5-15% of total transactions, and legitimate trial-to-paid conversions typically maintain a ratio under 3:1.

item.title: [DL-0080] Wallet Provisioning Following OTP Interception Indicator
item.description: Detects digital wallet provisioning events where the OTP or verification code was delivered within minutes of a social engineering indicator, such as an inbound call from a suspicious source, a phishing link click, or a smishing response. Legitimate wallet provisioning is typically self-initiated, with OTP-to-provisioning intervals of 30-120 seconds. When provisioning occurs within 15 seconds of OTP delivery, or when OTP delivery is preceded by a phishing or social engineering indicator within a 30-minute window, this strongly suggests automated interception-to-provision attack chains associated with digital wallet fraud (TP-0037). The card provisioning attempt is the critical disruption point where refined controls can prevent downstream contactless fraud.

item.title: [DL-0081] NFC Relay Geographic Impossibility on Contactless Transaction
item.description: Detects contactless (tap-to-pay) transactions where the POS terminal location is geographically impossible given the cardholder's last known location. When a contactless transaction occurs at a POS terminal more than 100 kilometers from the cardholder's most recent authenticated activity (mobile banking login, ATM withdrawal, or prior in-person transaction) within a timeframe that makes physical travel impossible, it indicates NFC relay (ghost-tapping) or unauthorized wallet token use. This rule specifically targets the Phase 4 execution stage of digital wallet fraud and NFC relay attacks (TP-0037), where money mules conduct contactless purchases using relayed card data at POS terminals geographically distant from the legitimate cardholder.
