item.title: [DL-0082] Ghost-Tap Multi-Terminal Contactless Velocity Anomaly
item.description: Detects multiple contactless transactions from the same wallet token or card credential across multiple distinct POS terminals within a short timeframe. Normal cardholder behavior produces a maximum of 2-3 contactless transactions per hour across different terminals during shopping activity. NFC relay (ghost-tapping) operations using tools such as SuperCardX, NFCGate, Hyper NFC, or Valkirie NFC enable simultaneous contactless transactions at multiple POS terminals by relaying stolen card data to multiple money mule devices. This rule detects the Phase 4 execution pattern of TP-0037 where the same wallet token appears at 3 or more distinct POS terminals within 30 minutes, a pattern that is physically impossible for a single cardholder and pathognomonic for NFC relay fraud.

item.title: [DL-0083] Card Testing Micro-Authorization Velocity Spike
item.description: Detects high velocity of sub-dollar ($0.01-$0.99) authorization attempts from the same merchant or source against multiple distinct card numbers, a pattern characteristic of automated card testing operations. Recorded Future's 2025 report identified over 1,350 tester merchant accounts, with 94% being newly registered merchants. Normal merchant sub-dollar authorization rates are under 0.5% of total authorizations. Card testing operations generate authorization streams where sub-dollar transactions dominate, decline rates exceed 70%, and unique card numbers per source per hour reach 50-500+. This rule targets Phase 4 of TP-0038, detecting the execution of automated card validation at scale through micro-authorization patterns that deviate from legitimate merchant transaction profiles.

item.title: [DL-0084] BIN Enumeration Sequential Card Number Attack
item.description: Detects sequential or near-sequential card number authorization attempts sharing the same Bank Identification Number (BIN) prefix with incremental variation in the remaining digits. BIN enumeration attacks generate valid card numbers by iterating through possible combinations within a BIN range, validating each against live payment infrastructure through sub-dollar authorization requests. Sequential card numbers from the same BIN prefix have a zero false positive rate for legitimate merchants — this pattern is exclusively associated with fraudulent enumeration. Recorded Future's 2025 report documents BIN attacks as a primary method for generating valid card credentials for downstream fraud, with enumerated cards feeding into card testing (TP-0038), digital wallet provisioning (TP-0037), and card-not-present fraud operations. This rule targets Phase 4 of TP-0038.

item.title: [DL-0085] Agent Intent Manipulation — Purchase Divergence from User Intent
item.description: Detects transactions initiated by AI agents where the product or service purchased diverges significantly from the user's stated intent or historical purchasing patterns, or where the receiving merchant is flagged as high-risk. This rule targets Phase 3 (Positioning) of agentic commerce fraud, where threat actors manipulate agent purchasing intent to redirect transactions to attacker-controlled merchants or execute purchases that do not reflect the consumer's actual desires. Key indicators include purchases in product categories the user has never engaged with, transactions at merchants created within the last 30 days, transaction amounts exceeding 3x the user's historical average, and merchants with elevated risk scores.

item.title: [DL-0086] Agent Transaction Velocity Anomaly
item.description: Detects AI agent-initiated transactions at velocities exceeding human purchasing patterns, including multiple purchases per minute and simultaneous multi-merchant purchases within a single agent session. This rule targets Phase 4 (Execution) of agentic commerce fraud, where compromised or manipulated agents execute unauthorized transactions at machine speed. Normal agent purchasing velocity is 1-5 purchases per user session with 2-15 minutes of comparison shopping per purchase. Velocities exceeding 10x human baseline (more than 5 transactions per minute or purchases across more than 3 merchants within a 60-second window) suggest automated fraud exploitation rather than legitimate agent-assisted shopping.

item.title: [DL-0087] BNPL Account Opening Risk Signal Cluster
item.description: Detects BNPL account applications exhibiting multiple risk signals indicative of synthetic identity fraud. Specifically targets accounts opened with email domains less than 30 days old, minimal digital footprint (score below 0.2), and patterns consistent with emulator-based mass account creation. BNPL providers using soft-check-only approval processes are particularly vulnerable to synthetic identities that pass initial verification but exhibit these digital footprint anomalies. This rule supports detection at Phase 2 of TP-0040 by identifying high-risk onboarding patterns before the synthetic identity progresses to credit grooming and multi-provider stacking.

item.title: [DL-0088] BNPL Multi-Provider Application Velocity
item.description: Detects identities applying to three or more distinct BNPL providers within a 72-hour window, a pattern characteristic of multi-provider stacking operations. Legitimate consumers rarely apply to more than two BNPL providers within a week. Synthetic identity rings exploit the absence of cross-bureau BNPL loan reporting to accumulate $3,000-$15,000 in aggregate exposure across providers while each provider sees only their individual exposure. This rule requires consortium-level data sharing to be effective, as individual providers cannot detect cross-provider application velocity in isolation. At Phase 3 of TP-0040, multi-provider stacking represents the critical positioning step before coordinated bust-out execution.

item.title: [DL-0089] BNPL Spending Step-Up to Limit Bust-Out Pattern
item.description: Detects the characteristic spending escalation pattern of BNPL bust-out fraud, where accounts begin with small purchases (under $50) during a credit grooming phase, then rapidly escalate to purchases consuming 85% or more of the available credit limit within 14 days. This pattern distinguishes synthetic bust-out operations from legitimate consumer behavior, where spending typically ramps gradually over weeks to months. Recorded in organized rings deploying 50-1,000+ synthetic identities, the grooming-to-bustout transition represents the highest-confidence detection window for TP-0040 Phase 4 execution, as the sharp behavioral shift from conservative to aggressive spending is difficult for fraudsters to avoid without sacrificing the speed required for coordinated multi-provider bust-out.

item.title: [DL-0090] BNPL Item-Not-Received Claim Velocity
item.description: Detects accounts filing three or more item-not-received (INR) claims within a 90-day rolling window where the average disputed order value exceeds $300. Legitimate INR dispute rates are under 1% of orders, with most disputes involving genuine delivery failures. Organized phantom delivery fraud and friendly fraud operations systematically file INR claims after receiving goods, targeting high-value orders to maximize returns. This rule supports TP-0040 Phase 4 detection by identifying accounts exhibiting claim patterns consistent with organized INR abuse rather than genuine delivery issues. The $300 average threshold filters out low-value legitimate disputes while capturing the high-value targeting characteristic of organized fraud.

item.title: [DL-0091] BNPL Cross-Account Device Clustering
item.description: Detects four or more distinct BNPL accounts created from or accessed by the same device fingerprint within a 30-day window, indicating potential synthetic identity ring activity or account farming operations. Normal BNPL usage involves 1-2 accounts per device over 12 months. Emulator-based mass account opening tools with device fingerprint spoofing can create dozens of accounts per day from a single physical device, but sophisticated device fingerprinting systems can detect emulator signatures and fingerprint collision patterns. This rule supports TP-0040 Phase 3 detection by identifying device-level clustering that precedes multi-provider stacking and coordinated bust-out.

item.title: [DL-0092] RDGA Registration Timing Pattern Detection
item.description: Detects clusters of domain registrations exhibiting algorithmically regular timing intervals in zone file diffs, a hallmark of Registered Domain Generation Algorithm (RDGA) infrastructure provisioning. Legitimate bulk registrations by brand protection services or hosting providers typically show irregular, human-driven timing patterns. RDGA tooling operates programmatically, producing registration bursts with low standard deviation in inter-registration intervals. This rule alerts when a cluster of newly registered domains exceeds a size threshold and the inter-registration timing standard deviation falls below a regularity threshold, indicating automated generation. Supports TP-0041 Phase 2 detection of RDGA-based initial access infrastructure staging.

item.title: [DL-0093] RDGA Nameserver Clustering Anomaly
item.description: Detects disproportionate concentration of newly registered domains pointing to the same nameserver infrastructure within a 24-hour window. RDGA operators typically provision hundreds or thousands of domains but anchor them to a small set of nameservers they control, creating a fan-in pattern that is statistically anomalous compared to legitimate registrar or hosting provider distributions. Legitimate nameservers serving large numbers of new domains tend to be well-known hosting or registrar nameservers with established reputation. This rule identifies nameserver endpoints receiving an abnormal influx of newly registered domain delegations, filtering out known hosting infrastructure. Supports TP-0041 Phase 2 detection of RDGA nameserver infrastructure consolidation.

item.title: [DL-0094] RDGA Registrar Concentration Anomaly
item.description: Detects anomalous concentration of new domain registrations at a single registrar that share lexical similarity patterns and nameserver infrastructure, indicating RDGA-driven bulk registration campaigns. Threat actors frequently exploit registrars with weak abuse controls, automated APIs, or low-cost bulk pricing to register large volumes of algorithmically generated domains. This rule correlates three signals: high registration volume at a single registrar, lexical similarity among the registered domain names (e.g., consonant-vowel patterns, character n-gram overlap, or string edit distance clustering), and shared nameserver delegation. The combination of these factors distinguishes RDGA activity from legitimate bulk registration by portfolio investors or brand protection services. Supports TP-0041 Phase 2 detection of registrar abuse for RDGA infrastructure provisioning.

item.title: [DL-0095] TDS Redirect Chain Depth Anomaly
item.description: Detects HTTP redirect chains (302, 301, or JavaScript-based redirects) exceeding a depth threshold where intermediate nodes are newly registered domains or have low reputation scores, indicating Traffic Distribution System (TDS) abuse. Legitimate web redirects rarely exceed 3 hops and typically traverse well-known CDN, analytics, or marketing infrastructure. TDS chains commonly use 4-7 or more hops through disposable intermediary domains to obfuscate the final destination, evade URL blocklists, and enable real-time traffic steering. Each hop in a TDS chain may perform user-agent filtering, geolocation checks, or bot detection before forwarding. This rule correlates redirect depth with domain age and reputation of intermediate nodes to distinguish malicious TDS chains from legitimate multi-hop redirects. Supports TP-0042 Phase 3 detection of TDS positioning and traffic funneling infrastructure.

item.title: [DL-0096] TDS Cloaking Behavior Detection
item.description: Detects domains serving divergent content based on visitor attributes such as geolocation, device fingerprint, or user agent, a technique known as cloaking. TDS operators serve benign or empty content to security scanner user agents (e.g., Googlebot, bingbot, crawlers), datacenter IP ranges, and known security vendor IP addresses, while delivering redirects or malicious content to residential IP addresses and consumer device fingerprints. This rule identifies cloaking by correlating response divergence across multiple request profiles to the same URL: when a domain returns substantially different HTTP response codes, content lengths, or redirect targets for scanner versus residential visitor profiles within a detection window, it indicates intentional cloaking. Supports TP-0042 Phase 3 detection of TDS cloaking used to evade automated threat scanning and URL reputation systems.

item.title: [DL-0097] TDS Shared Infrastructure Correlation
item.description: Detects domains from different apparent campaigns sharing hosting infrastructure, nameservers, or registration patterns — indicating a common TDS operator serving multiple affiliates. This rule performs graph-based correlation by identifying domains resolving to the same IP CIDR block with different registrant information but similar registration timing. TDS operators frequently reuse backend infrastructure across campaigns while rotating customer-facing domains, creating detectable infrastructure overlap patterns. Shared nameserver configurations, co-located IP assignments within the same /24 CIDR, and registration timestamps clustered within hours are strong indicators of centralized TDS management across ostensibly independent fraud campaigns.

item.title: [DL-0098] AI-Generated Domain Lexical Pattern Detection
item.description: Detects domain registrations exhibiting lexical patterns consistent with AI-generated names: natural-language-like domain names that are grammatically plausible but not established brands, unusual TLD selection patterns, and registration in bulk with similar lexical characteristics. Large language models can produce domain names that bypass traditional DGA detection because they use real words and plausible constructions rather than random character strings. This rule identifies clusters of newly registered domains sharing lexical similarity scores above threshold, exhibiting natural-language n-gram distributions, and registered through the same registrar within a compressed time window. AI-generated domain portfolios tend to follow detectable stylistic patterns such as consistent word-count, hyphenation style, and semantic category clustering that distinguish them from organic registrations.

item.title: [DL-0099] Bulk Let's Encrypt Certificate Issuance Clustering
item.description: Detects clusters of Let's Encrypt certificate issuances for domains sharing nameserver or registrar characteristics within a short time window. RDGA and AI-generated campaigns frequently provision certificates in bulk immediately after registration to enable HTTPS on fraudulent landing pages and phishing sites. Legitimate bulk certificate issuance typically occurs through established organizations with consistent registration history. This rule identifies anomalous spikes in certificate issuance where multiple domains share infrastructure indicators such as common nameservers, registrar, or IP allocation, and certificates are issued within hours of domain registration. The combination of rapid registration-to-certificate timing and shared infrastructure strongly indicates coordinated fraudulent domain provisioning for campaign deployment.

item.title: [DL-0100] Zone File Daily Diff Anomaly Detection
item.description: Detects anomalous patterns in daily zone file diffs: unusual volume of new registrations in a single TLD, concentration of registrations at specific registrars, or patterns suggesting algorithmic generation including lexical similarity, sequential naming, and entropy clustering. Zone file diffs provide a ground-truth view of new domain registrations across gTLDs and many ccTLDs. Fraudulent campaigns using RDGA, TDS, or AI-generated domain strategies produce detectable statistical anomalies in daily diff data — particularly registrar concentration spikes, abnormal per-TLD registration volumes, and clusters of domains with similar character distribution or word structure. This rule establishes rolling baselines for registrar-TLD combinations and alerts when daily new registration counts exceed three standard deviations from the 30-day rolling mean, or when entropy analysis reveals clustering indicative of algorithmic or template-based domain generation.

item.title: [DL-0101] State-Criminal Shared Infrastructure Overlap
item.description: Detect when IP addresses, nameservers, or hosting infrastructure previously attributed to state-sponsored threat actors begin hosting domains or services associated with criminal campaigns (or vice versa). Uses graph-based detection to identify shared IP CIDR blocks, nameserver overlap, and temporal proximity of domain registrations. State-criminal convergence represents an emerging threat where nation-state infrastructure is repurposed for financially motivated crime, or criminal bulletproof hosting serves dual-use purposes for both espionage and fraud operations. This detection correlates threat intelligence attribution data with passive DNS records and infrastructure registration metadata to surface shared hosting patterns across historically distinct threat actor categories.

item.title: [DL-0102] Sanctions Designation Infrastructure Migration
item.description: Detect infrastructure migration patterns following OFAC sanctions designations. Domains previously resolving to sanctioned entity IP ranges migrate to new hosting within 7-30 days of designation, retaining similar DNS configurations but different IP blocks. Tracks Aeza to Smart Digital/Datavice and Garantex to Grinex migration patterns. Sanctions designations trigger predictable infrastructure migration behavior where sanctioned entities rapidly move domains and services to new IP ranges while preserving nameserver configurations, MX records, and SSL certificate patterns. This detection correlates OFAC designation dates with zone file diffs and passive DNS records to identify domains that migrate from sanctioned IP ranges to new hosting within the expected evasion window, flagging infrastructure that retains structural DNS similarity despite IP block changes.

item.title: [DL-0103] Stablecoin Settlement Pattern Anomaly
item.description: Detect stablecoin transaction patterns consistent with sanctions evasion settlement. Identifies Monday-Friday volume surges with weekend drops (business settlement pattern), transaction clustering to known no-KYC exchange addresses, and volume patterns matching the A7A5 ruble-backed stablecoin profile. Sanctions evasion through stablecoin settlement produces distinctive temporal patterns that mirror traditional business settlement cycles rather than typical retail crypto trading behavior. The weekday-to-weekend volume ratio, combined with clustering of transactions to addresses associated with no-KYC exchanges, provides a high-confidence signal for institutional sanctions evasion activity. This detection establishes rolling baselines for address-level volume patterns and alerts when weekday-weekend ratios and exchange clustering metrics exceed defined thresholds.

item.title: [DL-0104] BPH Rebranding Chain Detection
item.description: Detect bulletproof hosting providers that rebrand following law enforcement or sanctions action. Identifies new hosting entities advertising the same IP ranges, same BGP ASN prefixes, or same upstream transit providers as recently sanctioned or seized BPH operations. Tracks the Garantex to Grinex and Aeza to Smart Digital/Datavice patterns. Bulletproof hosting providers under sanctions or law enforcement pressure follow predictable rebranding patterns — registering new corporate entities while retaining the same underlying network infrastructure. BGP route announcements, IP range allocations, and upstream transit provider relationships persist across rebrandings, providing durable detection signals. This rule monitors for new hosting entities that share ASN prefixes, IP CIDR blocks, or transit provider relationships with recently sanctioned or seized BPH operations within a 90-day window following enforcement action.

item.title: [DL-0105] Election-Cycle Domain Registration Spike
item.description: Detect anomalous increases in domain registrations containing financial institution brand names or financial services keywords during election periods. Compares registration volumes against a 90-day rolling baseline, alerting on 3x+ increases within 30 days of scheduled elections. Integrates with election calendar data for predictive detection.

item.title: [DL-0106] Sanctions-Announcement Infrastructure Correlation
item.description: Detect correlations between OFAC/EU sanctions announcements and subsequent infrastructure changes. Identifies new domain registrations by sanctioned entity-linked registrars, IP block migrations, and new BGP announcements from previously quiet ASNs within 14 days of sanctions designation.

item.title: [DL-0107] Politically-Motivated DDoS Financial Sector Targeting
item.description: Detect Layer 7 DNS attack patterns targeting financial services infrastructure that correlate with geopolitical event timelines. Differentiates politically motivated DDoS from criminal extortion DDoS by examining claim attribution (Telegram channel claims), target selection patterns (geopolitically aligned targets), and timing correlation with political events.

item.title: [DL-0108] Pig Butchering Domain Infrastructure Clustering
item.description: Detect clusters of domains exhibiting pig butchering investment platform characteristics: similar page structures, cryptocurrency wallet integration, registration through privacy-protected registrars, hosted on known scam compound infrastructure IP ranges. Documents Funnull-pattern CNAME clustering.

item.title: [DL-0109] Scam Compound Cryptocurrency Payment Infrastructure
item.description: Detect domain clusters with cryptocurrency payment page patterns (wallet address display, QR code generation, transaction verification) registered in bulk through shared registrar/nameserver infrastructure.

item.title: [DL-0110] BPH IP Block Migration Post-Sanctions
item.description: Detect IP address blocks previously associated with sanctioned or seized BPH providers appearing under new BGP announcements from different ASNs. Track continuity of malicious hosting through IP block ownership changes.

item.title: [DL-0111] Cloud Provider IP Abuse for BPH Resale
item.description: Detect patterns consistent with legitimate cloud provider IP blocks being resold for BPH: unusual CNAME density (100+ domains per IP), diverse domain registrants sharing the same cloud IP range, and high abuse-report-to-domain ratios. Documents Funnull-pattern indicators (332K domains across 548 CNAMEs).

item.title: [DL-0112] CNAME Clustering for DGA Domain Networks
item.description: Detect anomalous CNAME record density where hundreds or thousands of apparently unrelated domains share CNAME chains terminating at a small number of infrastructure endpoints. Indicates centrally managed infrastructure reusing cloud or CDN providers for mass domain hosting.

item.title: [DL-0113] CMLN Wallet Cluster Velocity
item.description: Detect cryptocurrency wallet clusters exhibiting CMLN operational characteristics: high transaction velocity (average processing time under 2 minutes), incoming transfers from multiple unrelated sources, and rapid outbound distribution to exchange or OTC wallets.

item.title: [DL-0114] No-KYC Exchange Off-Ramp Pattern
item.description: Detect cryptocurrency flows matching the DPRK 45-day laundering cycle pattern: initial rapid distancing through DeFi protocols (days 1-5), integration through no-KYC exchanges (days 5-14), and off-ramping through Chinese OTC brokers (days 20-45). Temporal pattern matching against known laundering cycle timelines.

item.title: [DL-0115] DaaS Platform Transaction Pattern
item.description: Detect cryptocurrency transactions matching Deepfake-as-a-Service (DaaS) subscription patterns: recurring payments of $100-$1,000/month to wallets associated with known deepfake service providers, or one-time payments of $50-$500 for per-use deepfake generation services. These patterns indicate procurement of deepfake tooling used in downstream fraud operations including identity verification bypass and social engineering.

item.title: [DL-0116] Real-Time Face/Voice Changer Detection During Video Interview
item.description: Detect real-time face and voice changing artifacts during video conferencing sessions: (1) virtual camera driver interception via OBS Virtual Camera, ManyCam, or DeepFaceLive, (2) audio spectral anomalies indicating synthetic voice generation or unnatural formant transitions, (3) temporal inconsistencies between lip movement and audio exceeding 200ms delta. These techniques are used by DPRK IT workers and other threat actors to impersonate identities during remote hiring interviews and ongoing employment.

item.title: [DL-0117] Multilingual Chatbot Scam Pattern Detection
item.description: Detect messaging patterns consistent with AI chatbot-initiated scam contact: (1) unusually consistent response timing with less than 2 second variance indicating automated replies, (2) scripted conversation progression matching known romance scam, investment scam, or pig-butchering templates, (3) language switching mid-conversation to target victims in their native language, (4) identical or near-identical phrasing across multiple reported conversation instances. These patterns are characteristic of scam compound operations using multilingual AI chatbots to scale social engineering.

item.title: [DL-0118] Automated Mule Account Creation Velocity
item.description: Detect automated account opening patterns indicative of mule account infrastructure buildout: (1) multiple applications originating from the same device fingerprint or IP address within a 24-hour window, (2) KYC document metadata anomalies such as identical creation timestamps or template-based formatting, (3) application completion in under 2 minutes suggesting automation, (4) absence of mouse movement or scroll events with rapid sequential field completion indicating bot-driven form filling.

item.title: [DL-0119] KYC Verification Bot Circumvention Detection
item.description: Detect automated circumvention of KYC identity verification processes: (1) liveness check submissions exhibiting synthetic face indicators such as GAN artifacts or uniform skin texture, (2) document photo lighting conditions inconsistent with selfie environment suggesting pre-captured or generated images, (3) multiple verification attempts from geographically dispersed IP addresses using the same identity documents, (4) session duration and interaction patterns matching known automation tooling.

item.title: [DL-0120] Investment TDS Geo-Routing to Legitimate Platform
item.description: Detect Traffic Distribution System (TDS) geo-routing patterns used in investment scam infrastructure: (1) same domain resolving to different IP addresses based on requester geography, (2) US-based visitors redirected to legitimate financial services such as eToro or Coinbase while non-US visitors are routed to newly registered scam domains, (3) CNAME records functioning as TDS routing mechanisms as observed in Savvy Seahorse campaigns. This evasion technique allows scam operators to avoid detection by security researchers and law enforcement in specific jurisdictions.

item.title: [DL-0121] DPRK Internal Platform Network Connection Detection
item.description: Detect connections to DPRK-associated internal collaboration platforms OConnect VPN and NetKey VPN, identified by Flare and IBM X-Force as tools used by DPRK IT workers: (1) VPN connections to known OConnect or NetKey IP address ranges, (2) DNS queries resolving OConnect or NetKey domains, (3) VPN protocol signatures matching OConnect or NetKey handshake patterns, particularly from endpoints that are simultaneously connected to corporate VPN infrastructure. Dual-VPN usage is a strong indicator of DPRK IT worker activity on compromised enterprise networks.

item.title: [DL-0122] Keitaro/Binom TDS Abuse Infrastructure Detection
item.description: Detect abuse of legitimate Traffic Distribution Systems Keitaro and Binom for fraud infrastructure: (1) HTTP redirect chains containing Keitaro tracking parameters such as click_id, campaign_id, and characteristic Keitaro URL path structures, (2) domains resolving to IP addresses associated with Keitaro or Binom hosting infrastructure, (3) redirect chain behavior patterns matching cloaking and visitor fingerprinting techniques used to evade security researchers while directing victims to investment scam landing pages.

item.title: [DL-0123] TAE Infrastructure Rotation Detection
item.description: Detect Threat Actor Ecosystem (TAE) infrastructure rotation patterns used by bulletproof hosting providers to evade sanctions and takedowns: (1) IP prefix transfers between related Autonomous Systems within short timeframes, (2) RIPE NCC resource reallocation to newly created organizations with minimal operational history, (3) BGP announcement changes matching known TAE rebranding patterns such as Aeza to Hypercore to NetCrafters, (4) threat density score spikes on newly announced prefixes indicating migration of malicious infrastructure to fresh address space.

item.title: [DL-0124] UCP Cart Mandate Gift Card Injection via Indirect Prompt Injection
item.description: Detects unauthorized gift card line items appended to UCP Cart Mandate payloads by AI shopping agents whose context has been compromised via indirect prompt injection. Threat actors create deals aggregator or coupon sites containing hidden payloads that reprogram the agent's memory during browsing. The agent then appends a hidden digital gift card line item to the Cart Mandate JSON-RPC payload with the recipient email set to an attacker-controlled address and display_status set to hidden. The additional cost may be disguised as Tax/Fees in the user's UI. This rule targets Phase 3-4 (Positioning/Execution) of the attack, detecting the presence of gift card items with suspicious recipient addresses or hidden display status in checkout payloads.

item.title: [DL-0125] UCP Returns Logic Hijacking — Void Return and Verify Step Bypass
item.description: Detects exploitation of the UCP returns state machine where AI agents skip the order.return.verify step and trigger settlement.refund.instant() using fraudulent tracking IDs (e.g., void-000). Threat actors embed hidden instructions in product page HTML metadata or invisible span tags that are ingested by the agent when it reads return instructions. The agent then processes the malicious command as a high-priority system update, bypassing return verification and issuing refunds without valid shipping confirmation. At scale, organized crime groups deploy bot farms to initiate thousands of void returns per hour, potentially liquidating a retailer's cash reserves. This rule targets Phase 4 (Execution) by detecting refund primitives triggered without proper verification, void tracking IDs, and anomalous refund velocity.

item.title: [DL-0126] Indirect Prompt Injection in UCP Agent Browsing Content
item.description: Detects indicators of indirect prompt injection payloads in web content encountered by UCP shopping agents during autonomous browsing. Because UCP agents are designed to autonomously browse, summarize and interact with merchant sites, they are highly susceptible to indirect prompt injection where the attack is not typed by the user but encountered by the agent while performing a task. Threat actors embed hidden payloads in deals aggregator sites, coupon pages, product listings, and merchant pages using techniques including invisible text, hidden HTML span tags, metadata-embedded instructions, and CSS-hidden content. These payloads target the agent's context window to reprogram behavior — appending hidden Cart Mandate line items, bypassing return verification steps, or redirecting transactions. This rule targets Phase 2 (Initial Access) by scanning agent-ingested content for prompt injection indicators before they can compromise agent behavior.

item.title: [DL-0127] TDS URL Parameter Fingerprint Tracking Across Rotating Domains
item.description: Detects consistent URL query parameter patterns (TDS software behavioral signatures) appearing across multiple rotating domains, indicating a single TDS operator managing infrastructure through domain rotation. TDS operators require consistent parameter schemas to route traffic between affiliates, track conversions, and attribute payouts — these parameters are the TDS internal API contract visible in redirect URLs even when domain names rotate. The VexTrio TDS was tracked for years via its distinctive ?u=&o= query parameter format before corporate attribution was achieved (Black Hat USA 2025, Infoblox). This rule identifies recurring parameter fingerprints across newly registered or rapidly rotating domains as indicators of TDS infrastructure managed by a single operator.

item.title: [DL-0128] Blank Credit Card Subscription Fraud Pattern Detection
item.description: Detects patterns consistent with blank credit card subscription fraud as operated by VexTrio/Ad Trafficko and similar affiliate fraud platforms. In this scheme, affiliates deploy customizable credit card capture templates offering low-cost items ("Free iPhone, $1.99 shipping" or "Walmart gift card, $0.99 shipping"). Victims enter card details believing they are paying a nominal fee; the platform charges a higher amount ($9.99 typical) and enrolls them in recurring subscriptions generating ongoing charges. Affiliate payouts reach $120 per successful lead. This rule targets the transaction monitoring layer to identify: (1) initial nominal-amount card-not-present charges from newly registered or unknown merchants followed by recurring charges at higher amounts, (2) merchant descriptor patterns consistent with subscription enrollment services, (3) high chargeback ratios from merchants exhibiting these patterns. Source: Black Hat USA 2025 (Infoblox VexTrio deanonymization).

item.title: [DL-0129] Fake Mobile App Residential Proxy and Subscription Scam Detection
item.description: Detects indicators of fake mobile applications that function as residential proxies or subscription scams, as documented in the VexTrio fake app operations (Black Hat USA 2025, Infoblox). VexTrio operated fake mobile apps for 7-8 years through Google Play Store, Apple App Store, and third-party forums. Three categories: (1) Fake VPNs that route user traffic through residential proxy networks (making users unwitting proxy nodes) with keyword-scanning capabilities targeting banking and personal information, (2) Fake Android cleaners (device optimization tools), (3) Fake spam/notification protection apps that operate a self-referential scam cycle — after push notification abuse infects the victim browser (100-150 notifications/day), victim is served an ad for a "spam protection" app that requests permissions to disable browser notifications, displays fabricated "blocked" notification screens, then transitions to $6.99/week subscription after 24 hours. This rule detects network-level and endpoint-level indicators of these app categories.

item.title: [DL-0130] Rapid Enrollment-to-Billing Healthcare Provider Anomaly
item.description: Detects healthcare providers (DME suppliers, hospice agencies, home health companies, ABA therapy providers) that begin submitting claims at high volume within 30 days of Medicare/Medicaid enrollment. Operation Gold Rush (DOJ 2025) documented a Russian-Estonian TCO that acquired 30+ legitimate DME companies and immediately submitted $10.6 billion in fraudulent claims using stolen identities. The rapid enrollment-to-billing pattern is the highest-confidence indicator of fraudulent provider intent: legitimate providers typically require months to establish patient relationships, credentialing, and operational infrastructure before reaching significant billing volume. This rule flags providers billing >$100,000 within 30 days of enrollment, with additional risk scoring for providers concentrated in known high-fraud geographic areas and providers with high single-code billing ratios.

item.title: [DL-0131] Single-Code Billing Concentration and Impossible Day Healthcare Fraud
item.description: Detects two high-confidence healthcare billing fraud indicators: (1) Single-code billing concentration — providers billing overwhelmingly one HCPCS/CPT code, where a single code exceeds 80% of total claims. Operation Gold Rush documented a TCO that submitted $10.6 billion in fraudulent claims concentrated on urinary catheters and continuous glucose monitors. Legitimate providers bill across diverse code sets reflecting varied patient needs. (2) Impossible day billing — providers billing more than 24 hours of procedures in a single calendar day, a mathematical impossibility indicating phantom billing or systematic upcoding. Both patterns are documented in DOJ 2025 National Healthcare Fraud Takedown prosecutions and CrimsonVector Security threat analysis. Source: CrimsonVector Security March 2026; DOJ Operation Gold Rush June 2025.

item.title: [DL-0132] Ghost Patient Claims and Geographic Provider Clustering Detection
item.description: Detects two healthcare fraud patterns: (1) Ghost patient claims — Medicare/Medicaid claims submitted for deceased, incarcerated, or relocated beneficiaries who could not have received the billed services. Operation Gold Rush exploited over 1 million stolen American identities including elderly and disabled individuals. (2) Geographic provider clustering — ZIP codes with anomalous concentrations of healthcare providers and high average billing per provider, indicating shell company clustering. LA County has 1,923 registered hospice providers (more than 36 states combined), with 7 of 14 entities in one LA plaza having zero CMS data. GAO reports found approximately 22% of practice locations in PECOS were potentially ineligible including UPS Store mailboxes and vacant addresses. Source: CrimsonVector Security March 2026; DOJ 2025 National Healthcare Fraud Takedown; GAO-15-448.

item.title: [DL-0133] Recovery Fraud Contact Pattern — Payments from Recent Fraud Victims to Unfamiliar Recipients
item.description: Detects potential recovery fraud by identifying payments from customers who filed fraud complaints within the preceding 90 days to previously unseen recipient accounts. Recovery fraud operators re-contact prior fraud victims posing as recovery agents, lawyers, or government officials, extracting additional fees for purported fund recovery. This rule correlates complaint records with subsequent outbound payment activity to flag secondary victimization.

item.title: [DL-0134] Mass-Marketing Fraud Burst Calling Pattern — SIM Farm and Robodialling Detection
item.description: Detects burst patterns from potential SIM farm or robodialling infrastructure targeting customer phone numbers. Mass-marketing fraud infrastructure uses sequential phone numbers, short call durations (most calls rejected), and high-volume outbound calling to reach victims at scale. This rule identifies inbound calling patterns characteristic of organized boiler room operations, including sequential source number prefixes, short call duration clustering, and geographic origin mismatch between caller ID display and actual call routing.

item.title: [DL-0135] Long-Firm Credit Buildup Pattern — Steady Low Utilization Followed by Rapid Spike
item.description: Detects commercial accounts following a long-firm fraud pattern: steady low-value credit utilization for 6-12 months (building creditworthiness) followed by rapid escalation in credit utilization (the "burst"). Long-firm fraud involves organized criminal groups establishing businesses, building credit relationships, then exploiting that trust to defraud supply chain partners and trade finance banks. The artificially smooth buildup period followed by a discontinuous spike is the hallmark behavioral indicator.

item.title: [DL-0136] Staged Accident Claim Correlation — Shared Professional Enabler Network Detection
item.description: Detects potential organized crash-for-cash insurance fraud rings by identifying claims from multiple ostensibly unrelated accidents that share common professional enablers (same medical provider, legal representative, or repair shop). Organized insurance fraud rings rely on networks of corrupt professionals who process claims across multiple staged incidents. The shared professional enabler network is the most durable and detectable element of the ring, as replacing trusted corrupt professionals is harder than recruiting new participants.

item.title: [DL-0137] AiTM Session Token Replay Detection — User-Agent and IP Mismatch Post-MFA
item.description: Detects potential Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) session token replay by identifying User-Agent string or IP address mismatches between MFA completion events and subsequent session access events. AiTM phishing kits capture session tokens during MFA relay, then replay them from attacker infrastructure with different User-Agent/IP characteristics. Sekoia.io identified 11 major AiTM kits (Tycoon 2FA most prevalent: 1,200+ domains, 500K+ organizations/month). FIDO2 blocks 93.9% of AiTM campaigns.

item.title: [DL-0138] Post-Compromise Inbox Rule Manipulation — Rule Creation After New-IP Authentication
item.description: Detects inbox rule creation or modification within 24 hours of a sign-in from a previously unseen IP address. AiTM phishing kit operators create inbox rules within minutes of session hijack to redirect payment notifications, delete security alerts, and intercept colleague communications. Rules forwarding to external domains or deleting emails matching specific sender/subject patterns are high-confidence indicators of post-compromise activity.

item.title: [DL-0139] AI-Generated Phishing Content Stylometric Detection
item.description: Detects AI-generated phishing content using stylometric features. Research shows XGBoost with 60 stylometric features detects GPT-4o-generated phishing with 96% accuracy and 99% AUC. Key features: imperative verb count, clause density, first-person pronoun usage, urgency markers, authority indicators, sentiment manipulation, financial trigger words, and semantic inconsistency. DetectGPT achieves ~0.95 AUROC via zero-shot statistical signatures. This rule defines the feature extraction pipeline and scoring thresholds for deployment in email security and fraud communication analysis systems.

item.title: [DL-0140] Cialdini Persuasion Principle Scoring in Fraud Communications
item.description: Scores inbound communications (email, SMS, chat) for Cialdini's six principles of persuasion: Reciprocity, Consistency, Social Proof, Authority, Liking, and Scarcity. Research shows combining these features with BERT/SBERT embeddings improves phishing detection F1 by 2.62%. Communications exhibiting 3+ principles above threshold are flagged as high-probability social engineering. Directly applicable to romance fraud, investment scam, impersonation, and recovery fraud detection where psychological manipulation is the primary attack vector.

item.title: [DL-0141] SIM Swap Network-Level API Detection — Pre-MFA SIM Change Verification
item.description: Detects potential SIM swap attacks by querying network-level APIs before MFA code delivery. SIM swap fraud surged 1,055% in the UK (3,000 cases in 2024). Three network-level APIs provide the most effective detection: SIM Swap Check (has the SIM been changed recently?), Number Verification (is the number still assigned to the expected device?), and Call Forwarding Signal (is call forwarding active?). Correlating positive signals from these APIs with subsequent MFA authentication attempts provides high-confidence SIM swap detection.

item.title: [DL-0142] Crypto Token Rug Pull Early Warning — On-Chain and OSINT Indicators
item.description: Detects cryptocurrency rug pull / exit scam indicators using on-chain and OSINT signals. Rug pulls constituted 68% of all crypto scams in 2025 (350+ cases 2024). On-chain indicators: Uniswap liquidity removal >80% in single transaction, token holder concentration (top 5 holders >60%), contract functions with hidden mint/pause/ blacklist capabilities. OSINT indicators: social media silence after promotion burst, developer wallet activity cessation, Telegram/Discord channel deletion. Critical finding: OSINT signals precede on-chain anomalies by days or weeks.

item.title: [DL-0143] Employment Fraud Metadata Feature Detection
item.description: Detects fraudulent job postings using metadata features from the EMSCAD benchmark (18,000 samples). Key finding: when both telecommuting and company logo flags equal zero, there is a 92% probability of fraud. Geographic concentration patterns (e.g., Bakersfield 15:1 fake-to-real ratio) provide additional signal. DistilBERT+SMOTE models achieve strong results; DNNs reach ~98% accuracy. This rule implements the high-confidence metadata feature checks that require no NLP processing.

item.title: [DL-0144] Gift Card Balance Probing Velocity Detection
item.description: Detects automated gift card balance probing by monitoring balance check endpoints for high-velocity requests. NRF RFT FT1103 documents that fraudsters abuse legitimate balance check functions (web app, phone IVR) to identify funded cards from brute-forced or purchased card number lists. Detection signals include request velocity per IP/device, VoIP source numbers, off-hours timing, and device fingerprint anomalies. Gift card balance probing is a precursor to gift card redemption fraud, card merging, and resale monetization.

item.title: [DL-0145] Gift Card Merge and Transfer Anomaly Detection
item.description: Detects suspicious gift card merge and transfer activity indicating value consolidation from multiple illicit sources. NRF RFT FT1202 documents that fraudsters transfer value from multiple illicitly obtained gift cards to a single legitimate card — e.g., 20 cards with $5 merged into one $255 card. This consolidation is a key Control phase technique enabling subsequent monetization. Detection signals include merge velocity, source card count, and correlation with recent suspicious balance check activity.

item.title: [DL-0146] AiTM Session Token Replay — Same SessionId from Multiple IPs
item.description: Detects potential AiTM session token replay by identifying the same Entra ID SessionId appearing from multiple IP addresses within a short time window. In an AiTM attack, the phishing proxy IP and the attacker's actual replay IP both appear on the same session. This is the single strongest AiTM detection signal in Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs. Additional confidence comes from the error code sequence 50074 (MFA required) → 50140 (Keep Me Signed In) → 0 (success) in rapid succession with medium or high risk level.

item.title: [DL-0147] Sneaky 2FA Impossible Device Shift — User-Agent Mismatch per Auth Step
item.description: Detects the "impossible device shift" signature characteristic of Sneaky 2FA and related AiTM phishing kits. Sneaky 2FA uses different hardcoded User-Agent strings per authentication step — Safari on iOS for the Login:login step and Edge on Windows for the Login:resume step. This pattern is detectable via correlation of mismatched User-Agents within the same correlation ID within 10 minutes. This detection also catches Dadsec (missing User-Agent), Tycoon 2FA (rare User-Agent values), and W3LL OV6 (inconsistent UAs).

item.title: [DL-0148] Rockstar 2FA / FlowerStorm Application ID and User-Agent Detection
item.description: Detects sign-ins associated with the Rockstar 2FA and FlowerStorm AiTM phishing kits (Storm-1575 lineage) by matching the hardcoded Office365 Application ID and User-Agent string used by these kits. Rockstar 2FA and its successor FlowerStorm use the Office365 Application ID 72782ba9-4490-4f03-8d82-562370ea3566 combined with the hardcoded User-Agent string containing "WebView/3.0" — a high-fidelity detection signature with very low false positive rate. FlowerStorm surged within ~10 days of Rockstar 2FA's infrastructure collapse in November 2024.

item.title: [DL-0149] Smishing Triad Domain Pattern and iMessage/RCS Delivery Detection
item.description: Detects indicators of Smishing Triad phishing infrastructure including Darcula/Magic Cat domain patterns and Chenlun kit fingerprints. The Smishing Triad ecosystem has generated 194,000+ malicious domains targeting users in 121+ countries, compromising 884,000+ credit cards. Darcula domains follow a "com-" prefix pattern. Chenlun kits are fingerprinted by the presence of ResourceRedConfig.js and /ResourceConfig/urlConfig.json files. Detection also covers toll-scam lure patterns (E-ZPass, SunPass, FasTrak, I-Pass) commonly used in smishing campaigns.

item.title: [DL-0150] Post-AiTM Inbox Rule Manipulation — New Rules from Risky Sign-In
item.description: Detects inbox rule creation or modification in Exchange Online following a sign-in flagged with medium or high risk, or following authentication from a previously unseen IP address. Post-AiTM inbox rule manipulation is a characteristic Phase 3 (Positioning) technique: within minutes of session hijack, attackers create inbox rules to redirect or delete security alerts, payment notifications, and colleague communications. This detection correlates Exchange Online Unified Audit Log operations (New-InboxRule, Set-InboxRule, Set-Mailbox forwarding) with Entra ID risky sign-in events.

item.title: [DL-0151] Synthetic Identity Credit Utilization Spike — Low-and-Slow Buildup Followed by Bust-Out
item.description: Detects the characteristic synthetic identity bust-out pattern: prolonged low credit utilization (< 35% for 6+ months) followed by a rapid spike to near-maximum utilization (> 80%) within 30 days. Synthetic identity fraudsters nurture credit profiles over 12-24 months with steady payments and low utilization, then execute a coordinated bust-out where all available credit is maxed simultaneously. The Federal Reserve estimates synthetic identity fraud costs U.S. lenders $6B+ annually. The discontinuous utilization jump from a stable baseline is the hallmark behavioral indicator.

item.title: [DL-0152] Thin-File Identity Clustering — Shared Address, Phone, or Device Across New Applicants
item.description: Detects clusters of thin-file credit applicants sharing physical addresses, phone numbers, or device fingerprints — a hallmark indicator of synthetic identity ring activity. Fraud rings fabricate multiple synthetic identities that share infrastructure (mailing addresses, burner phones, devices used for applications). When 3+ new applicants with thin credit files (< 12 months history, < 3 tradelines) share an address, phone, or device within a 180-day window, this indicates coordinated identity fabrication rather than coincidental overlap. The Federal Reserve identifies address and device clustering as primary synthetic identity detection signals.

item.title: [DL-0153] Coordinated Bust-Out Timing — Simultaneous Max-Utilization Across Multiple Products
item.description: Detects coordinated bust-out execution where the same identity (or linked identities) max out credit across multiple products within a 72-hour window. Synthetic identity rings time their bust-out to extract maximum value before accounts are frozen: cash advances, balance transfers to controlled accounts, and high-value purchases for resale all occur within a narrow window. When 3+ credit products associated with the same identity show utilization above 90% within 72 hours, and at least one involves a cash advance or balance transfer, this is a high-confidence bust-out indicator.

item.title: [DL-0154] SSN Age and Issuance Mismatch — Synthetic Identity Indicator
item.description: Detects credit applications where the SSN characteristics are inconsistent with the applicant's stated identity — a primary indicator of synthetic identity fabrication. Key signals: (1) SSN issued after the applicant's date of birth suggests the SSN belongs to someone else (minors, immigrants, recently deceased), (2) post-2011 randomized SSNs that don't match SSA area number geography, (3) SSN first appearing at credit bureaus within the last 18 months combined with an applicant age > 25 (natural credit profiles start appearing at 18-22). The eCBSV (electronic Consent Based SSN Verification) service can confirm SSN-name-DOB matches, but adoption is inconsistent.

item.title: [DL-0155] First-Party Credit Buildup and Sudden Spike
item.description: Detects consumer accounts following a first-party fraud pattern: steady good payments for 6-12 months then sudden utilization spike and missed payments within 60 days. Unlike synthetic identity (TP-0003), the identity is real but the intent is fraudulent. First-party bust-out actors nurture credit profiles with consistent on-time payments and low utilization, then rapidly maximize available credit before abandoning the account. The transition from responsible usage to aggressive drawdown is the key behavioral signal. LexisNexis estimates first-party fraud now represents 36% of all detected fraud events globally.

item.title: [DL-0156] Never-Pay Pattern — Immediate Max Utilization with Zero Payments
item.description: Detects new credit accounts with immediate high utilization and zero payment activity after 60 days — classic "never-pay" first-party fraud where the consumer opens an account with no intent to pay. Unlike bust-out schemes that involve a credit nurturing phase, never-pay actors maximize utilization immediately after account opening and make no payments whatsoever. This pattern is distinguishable from legitimate new account activity because at least one billing cycle has passed with zero payment response. The never-pay variant accounts for a significant share of first-party fraud losses, particularly in unsecured credit products.

item.title: [DL-0157] Rapid Authorized User Addition Across Multiple Accounts
item.description: Detects the same individual being added as an authorized user across 3 or more credit accounts within 30 days. This technique is used in first-party bust-out and synthetic identity schemes to rapidly build credit history or gain access to multiple credit lines for coordinated bust-out. Authorized user tradelines inherit the primary account's payment history, allowing fraudsters to artificially inflate credit scores in weeks rather than months. When combined with subsequent high utilization, this pattern is a strong leading indicator of coordinated bust-out activity. The "piggybacking" of authorized user status is a well-documented credit manipulation technique exploited by both first-party fraudsters and synthetic identity rings.

item.title: [DL-0158] Document Metadata Anomaly — AI-Generated ID Document Detection
item.description: Detects submitted identity documents with metadata inconsistencies indicating AI generation or manipulation: PDF creation tools (Photoshop, GIMP, AI generators), timestamp manipulation (creation date after modification date), inconsistent DPI, missing EXIF data, font embedding anomalies. 85% of synthetic fraud now involves GenAI document fabrication. Underground services like OnlyFake and ProKYC produce photo-realistic government IDs for as little as $30, complete with simulated holograms and barcode data, but leave detectable metadata and structural artifacts that differ from genuine document scans.

item.title: [DL-0159] Facial Liveness Failure Pattern — Iterative Deepfake Tuning
item.description: Detects repeated liveness check failures from the same device followed by eventual success — indicates iterative deepfake tuning where fraudsters adjust their deepfake parameters until they pass liveness detection. Normal users fail once (bad lighting) and succeed quickly; attackers show a pattern of 3+ failures with improving scores. Real-time face-swap applications and pre-recorded deepfake videos are used to defeat challenges requiring head turns, blinking, or phrase repetition. The iterative improvement pattern — each attempt scoring higher than the last — is a strong indicator of adversarial tuning against the liveness detection model.

item.title: [DL-0160] Cross-Application Identity Collision — Same Biometric or Device Across Different Identities
item.description: Detects the same biometric template (face embedding), device fingerprint, or behavioral pattern appearing across applications submitted under different identity names. Fraudsters using AI-generated faces may reuse the same base model or device, creating detectable collisions in the biometric or device space. Even when AI-generated facial images appear visually distinct, the underlying face embedding vectors may cluster due to shared generative model artifacts. Similarly, device fingerprints and behavioral biometric profiles persist across sessions even when the presented identity changes, enabling cross-application correlation that reveals synthetic identity networks.

item.title: [DL-0161] AI Document Template Cluster — Identical Formatting Patterns Across Applications
item.description: Detects clusters of submitted ID documents sharing identical formatting artifacts, template structures, or AI generation signatures. AI document generators produce documents with consistent pixel-level artifacts, font embedding patterns, and template metadata even when the identity details differ. When 3+ documents from different applicants show template_similarity_score > 0.85, this indicates a common AI generator. Underground forgery services like OnlyFake successors use a limited number of document templates per jurisdiction, creating detectable clustering when multiple synthetic identities are onboarded through the same forgery pipeline. Template similarity analysis across the document corpus reveals these clusters even when individual documents pass automated verification checks.

item.title: [DL-0162] Check Washing — Altered Check Mobile Deposit with Duplicate or MICR Inconsistency
item.description: Detects mobile deposits of potentially washed or altered checks by identifying two key indicators: (1) the same check number deposited at multiple financial institutions within a short window, indicating duplicate deposit fraud, and (2) check amounts inconsistent with the MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) line data, suggesting the payee and amount fields were chemically washed and rewritten while the MICR line was preserved. FinCEN data shows check fraud SARs surged 200%+ from 2021-2023, driven by USPS mail theft and the ease of mobile deposit. Washed checks deposited via mobile apps exploit the lag between deposit and check clearing under Reg CC funds availability requirements. The Recorded Future 2025 report documented a geographic shift in stolen check activity toward the Midwest and suburban/rural USPS routes.

item.title: [DL-0163] Disability Insurance Fraud — Fabricated Medical Documentation Provider Anomaly
item.description: Detects patterns indicative of fabricated medical documentation supporting fraudulent disability claims by identifying two key signals: (1) a single medical provider billing across multiple claimants with identical or near-identical diagnosis codes (ICD-10), suggesting template-driven fabricated documentation rather than genuine clinical variation, and (2) claims supported by providers located outside the claimant's geographic area, indicating the claimant traveled specifically to a complicit provider or the documentation was fabricated remotely. DOJ prosecutions reveal organized disability fraud rings where complicit providers generate documentation for dozens of fictitious or exaggerated claims, with cumulative payouts in the millions. The long-tail nature of disability payments means a single fraudulent claim can generate $100,000+ in benefits before detection. Generative AI tools now enable fabrication of convincing medical documentation without provider collusion, representing an emerging escalation vector.

item.title: [DL-0164] Insider-Enabled Account Fraud — Employee Access Anomaly with Subsequent Account Changes
item.description: Detects financial institution employees accessing customer accounts outside their normal behavioral pattern, combined with subsequent account modifications — a hallmark of insider- enabled fraud. The rule identifies four converging anomaly signals: (1) account access occurring outside normal business hours for the employee's role, (2) access volume significantly exceeding the employee's baseline, (3) access to accounts not assigned to the employee's portfolio or branch, and (4) account changes (address, beneficiary, contact info, transaction limits) following the anomalous access. The ACFE estimates insider fraud accounts for 5% of organizational revenue globally, with an average detection time of 18 months. Financial institution insiders are particularly dangerous because they understand internal controls and operate below detection thresholds. This rule correlates UEBA access data with account modification logs to surface the positioning phase (CFPF P3) before funds are extracted.

item.title: [DL-0165] Business Identity Takeover — Rapid Signer, Address, and Banking Detail Changes on Established Account
item.description: Detects potential business identity takeover by identifying a cluster of critical account changes occurring within a short window on established commercial accounts. The rule flags accounts where authorized signer changes, business address updates, and banking detail modifications (routing/account number, wire instructions, or beneficiary changes) all occur within 14 days — a pattern strongly indicative of corporate hijacking. Threat actors impersonate legitimate businesses by filing fraudulent amendments with the Secretary of State to change registered agents or officers, then use the hijacked identity to modify banking relationships and extract funds. Established accounts (open 12+ months) are specifically targeted because they have built credit history and banking relationships that actors exploit. This pattern was heavily observed during pandemic-era PPP/EIDL fraud and continues to plague commercial lenders. Average commercial loan fraud via business identity theft ranges from $100K to $1M+.

item.title: [DL-0166] GenAI-Enhanced APP Fraud — Escalating Investment Payments to New Beneficiary
item.description: Detects the characteristic authorized push payment (APP) pattern associated with GenAI- enhanced investment fraud (pig butchering). The rule identifies customers making increasing payments to a newly added beneficiary with investment-related payment references, where payment velocity accelerates over a multi-week period. This pattern reflects the classic fattening-then-slaughter cycle: victims are groomed through AI-powered financial advisor personas and deepfake celebrity endorsements, make a small initial investment, see fabricated returns on fraudulent trading dashboards, and are progressively encouraged to invest larger amounts. The FBI IC3 reported $8.65 billion in investment fraud losses in 2025 (up from $6.57B in 2024) — the single largest fraud category. IC3 2025 data shows 72% of investment fraud payments flow through cryptocurrency, 19% via wire transfer/ACH, and 4% peer-to-peer. Chainalysis research shows AI-enabled investment scams extract 4.5x more revenue per operation ($3.2M average) compared to non-AI variants ($719K average). The rule targets the execution phase (P4) where escalating authorized payments represent the point of maximum financial exposure before funds are laundered through cryptocurrency mixing, DeFi protocols, or mule networks.

item.title: [DL-0167] Elder Financial Exploitation — New Payee Addition with Escalating Payment Amounts
item.description: Detects a multi-signal elder financial exploitation pattern: account holder aged 65 or older adds a new payee not present in their historical payment network, followed by escalating payment amounts to that payee over a rolling 30-day window. FBI IC3 reported $7.748B in elder fraud losses in 2025 (59% YoY increase from $4.885B in 2024), with 201,266 complaints from victims aged 60+. Crypto ATM/kiosk fraud disproportionately targets this cohort: 6,188 complaints and $257M in losses from 60+ victims alone. The convergence of advanced age, new payee addition, and escalating amounts is a hallmark of romance scams, tech support fraud, government impersonation, and caregiver exploitation — all of which follow a pattern of trust-building followed by increasing financial extraction. This rule targets Phase 4 (Execution) but the escalating pattern often indicates prolonged Phase 2/3 social engineering that has already been underway for weeks or months.

item.title: [DL-0168] Web3 Wallet Drainer — Malicious Token Approval to Drainer Contract
item.description: Detects wallet drainer approval phishing by identifying three high-confidence on-chain indicators: (1) token approval (approve() or increaseAllowance()) granting unlimited allowance to a contract address on known drainer threat feeds, (2) unlimited ERC-20 approvals to contracts deployed within the last 48 hours with no verified source code, or (3) rapid multi-token approvals (3+ distinct token contracts) from a single wallet to the same spender address within a 10-minute window — characteristic of automated DaaS kit multi-token harvesting. ScamSniffer reported $494M stolen via wallet drainers in 2024, with Inferno Drainer commanding 40-45% DaaS market share. The Permit/Permit2 gasless signature variant bypasses traditional on-chain approval monitoring; this rule covers the on-chain approve() path and Permit2 batch transfer events. Stolen assets are typically consolidated and bridged cross-chain within hours.

item.title: [DL-0169] Ghost Student Financial Aid Fraud — Multi-Signal Botnet Enrollment Detection
item.description: Detects ghost student financial aid fraud by correlating three botnet-driven enrollment indicators: (1) multiple FAFSA applications originating from the same device fingerprint or IP address within an enrollment cycle, (2) shared bank accounts across distinct financial aid applicants (multiple student IDs disbursing to the same routing/account number), or (3) financial aid disbursements from multiple student IDs flowing to the same beneficiary account or being withdrawn at the same ATM cluster. California community colleges flagged 31-34% of applications as potentially fraudulent, and Equifax reported preventing $180M in ghost student fraud in a single year. Ghost student botnets exploit open-enrollment admissions to submit hundreds of synthetic identity applications per cycle, file FAFSA for maximum Pell Grant eligibility ($7,395/year), and extract disbursements before census date attendance verification can trigger aid return requirements.

item.title: [DL-0170] Calendar Invite Injection Phishing — Mass External Calendar Event Creation from New Domains
item.description: Detects calendar injection phishing by identifying mass calendar invite creation from external sources targeting internal users, where the event body contains URLs and the organizer domain is recently registered (under 30 days) or on a high-abuse TLD. Attackers send emails containing .ics calendar attachments or Google Calendar invite links that auto-populate on victim calendars, bypassing email gateway filtering that focuses on message body and attachment analysis. An observed March 2026 campaign delivered 6,000+ emails across 10 sender domains (9 RDGA-generated on .cyou/.sbs/.click TLDs) with antivirus renewal and meeting invite lures. Calendar events persist after email deletion and re-surface via reminder notifications, creating a delayed-action social engineering vector. Recently created organizer accounts (under 7 days) sending calendar invites to 5+ internal recipients are additionally flagged as high-confidence indicators.

item.title: [DL-0171] QR Code Payment Fraud (Quishing) — Malicious QR Destination to Credential Harvesting Infrastructure
item.description: Detects quishing attacks by identifying emails or messages containing QR code images where the encoded URL resolves to a recently registered domain (under 30 days), a known URL shortener redirecting to a credential harvesting page, or a domain impersonating postal services or banking institutions. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents a European modus operandi where fraudsters send fake QR codes claiming payment is available at a post office, routing victims through a fake postal site to a cloned bank login page. In a documented case, USD 110,000 was stolen through this method. The attack exploits a fundamental QR code UX gap: unlike hyperlinks, QR codes do not display a destination URL before the victim commits to following them. The subsequent 2FA device enrollment step converts credential capture into persistent account takeover, making real-time detection at the email/content analysis layer critical before the victim scans.

item.title: [DL-0172] Sextortion-Investment Hybrid Fraud — Small Payment Escalation to Crypto Addresses with Communication Pattern Shift
item.description: Detects the sextortion-investment hybrid fraud pattern where a victim makes initial small payments followed by escalating amounts to cryptocurrency addresses, with the communication pattern showing a transition from social/romantic interaction to financial urgency. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents this as a globally escalating pattern where scam centre operators systematically pivot from romance/investment scripts to sextortion as a scripted operational fallback. The hallmark behavioral signature is a first-ever crypto transaction within 30 days of a new social media contact, followed by rapid escalation in both payment frequency and amount, often accompanied by messaging patterns shifting from casual/romantic to urgent/threatening language. The hybrid structure maximizes total extraction while suppressing victim reporting through shame and blackmail leverage.

item.title: [DL-0173] Vehicle Export Financing Fraud — Auto Loan Followed by Rapid Title Transfer or Export with Active Lien
item.description: Detects the vehicle export financing fraud pattern where an auto loan application is approved and the financed vehicle undergoes rapid title transfer or appears in export documentation while the loan remains active and the lien is outstanding. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents this as a growing transnational fraud scheme first detected in North America in early 2024, where criminal networks use identity theft and straw buyers to obtain auto loans for high-value vehicles, then export them overseas before lenders detect fraud. The critical detection window is the period between vehicle delivery and export — often as short as 7-21 days. Key indicators include high-value vehicles (>$30,000) with high LTV ratios, fewer than 3 loan payments made, title transfer events within 60 days of origination, and GPS telematics showing vehicle departure from the borrower's stated area toward port cities or border crossings. The structural delay between loan default and fraud detection is the primary vulnerability exploited by these networks.

item.title: [DL-0174] Crypto Fraud-Terrorism/Narco Financing Nexus — Sanctions-Exposed Wallets and Peel Chain Patterns Through Mixing Services
item.description: Detects the crypto-terror/narco financing nexus pattern where transactions flow to wallets with known OFAC/sanctions exposure, or exhibit peel chain patterns through cryptocurrency mixing services followed by consolidation to designated entity-linked addresses. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment documents two confirmed manifestations: (1) a USD 150 million cryptocurrency fraud scheme linked to Tren de Aragua laundering drug trafficking and extortion proceeds across Chile, Colombia, Venezuela, and the Iberian Peninsula; and (2) Operation Catalyst, which uncovered a USD 562 million crypto Ponzi scheme affecting 100,000+ victims across 17 countries with wallet-level links to terrorism financing in Central Africa. The detection logic targets three signatures: direct transactions to OFAC SDN-listed wallet addresses within 2 hops, peel chain patterns where funds are split into decreasingly small amounts through mixing services before reconsolidation, and co-mingling indicators where platform wallets receive both retail investor deposits and large round-number inflows from high-risk wallet clusters. This rule operates at critical severity given the terrorism and narcotics financing implications and associated OFAC blocking obligations.

item.title: [DL-0175] Organized Insurance Claims Fraud — Shared Professional Enablers and Claim Timing Clustering Around Policy Inception
item.description: Detects organized insurance claims fraud patterns where the same claimant or provider appears across multiple claims with shared professional enablers (medical provider, legal representative, repair shop), or where claim timing is clustered around policy inception. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment identifies insurance fraud — notably car and medical insurance claims — as escalating globally, with Europe most impacted: the UK recorded a 25% spike in motor insurance fraud in early 2025, France detected nearly USD 1 billion in fraud in 2024, and German insurers flagged 10% of claims as suspicious with annual losses exceeding USD 7 billion. The detection logic targets two primary signatures: (1) network analysis identifying claimants, providers, legal representatives, or repair shops appearing across multiple claims — indicating an organized fraud ring with division of labor; and (2) temporal analysis identifying claims filed within 90 days of policy inception with high severity, which indicates opportunistic application fraud followed by immediate fraudulent claim filing. The combination of shared enablers and inception-proximate timing is a strong indicator of organized ring activity.

item.title: [DL-0176] Organized Counterfeit Goods and Non-Delivery Fraud Network — High Dispute Merchant Accounts with Drop Location Clustering and Below-Market Pricing
item.description: Detects organized counterfeit goods and non-delivery fraud network activity by identifying merchant accounts exhibiting multiple fraud indicators simultaneously: high chargeback/dispute rates, shipping addresses clustered at known drop locations, product listings priced significantly below market value, and seller account age under 90 days with disproportionately high transaction volume. The UNODC Organized Fraud Issue Paper (2024) documents this as the most prevalent fraud category by volume, with organized criminal groups operating multi-site networks backed by dedicated money laundering infrastructure, recruited money mules, and counterfeit supply chains. Case studies from Romania, Germany, and the US show OCGs adopting formal business structures — suppliers, distribution centers, online retailers — to deceive payment providers and scale operations. The detection logic combines four signals: (1) dispute rate exceeding 2% of transactions indicating non-delivery or counterfeit complaints; (2) shipping address concentration at drop locations or mail receiving services; (3) product pricing 30%+ below market benchmarks; and (4) new seller accounts (<90 days) with anomalously high listing and transaction volume. Any two of these four indicators in combination warrant investigation.

item.title: [DL-0177] Magecart WebSocket Card Data Exfiltration — Payment Page to Recently Registered Domain
item.description: Detects Magecart-style card data exfiltration via WebSocket connections from e-commerce checkout or payment pages to recently registered domains (< 90 days) that masquerade as legitimate services (analytics, CDN, jQuery). The ANY.RUN "Banks Magecart Campaign" (March 2026) documented a 24+ month campaign across 100+ domains targeting the Redsys payment system (Spain), PayPlug SAS, and generic Visa/Mastercard flows. The attack uses a multi-stage injection model: (1) obfuscated loader injected into site scripts, (2) rotating domains deliver secondary payloads, (3) DOM monitoring conceals legitimate payment buttons and injects fake payment interfaces, (4) WebSocket connections (wss://<c2>/?token=<base64>) exfiltrate full card data (BIN, PAN, expiry, CVV). WebSocket is chosen specifically to reduce visibility in traditional HTTP-based security monitoring. Detection combines three signals: WebSocket connection from a payment/checkout page context, destination domain registered within 90 days, and domain name pattern masquerading as a legitimate service (analytics, CDN, jQuery, caching). The confirmed IOC domain list from the campaign uses registrar NICENIC INTERNATIONAL GROUP, identified by Silent Push as a bulletproof registrar.

item.title: [DL-0178] Bulletproof Hosting ASN Connection Correlation — Traffic to Known BPH Networks
item.description: Detects DNS resolution or network connections to IP addresses within known bulletproof hosting (BPH) Autonomous System Number (ASN) ranges, domains registered via the NiceNIC registrar, or domains using Dynamic DNS providers such as afraid.org. Silent Push (2025) documented 200+ BPH providers controlling approximately 1 million IP addresses globally. This rule correlates network traffic against a curated list of BPH ASNs identified through abuse pattern analysis, including providers with high DGA domain density, disposable abuse contact emails, shell company registrations in permissive jurisdictions, and self-declared bulletproof hosting marketing. Additionally, the rule flags domains registered through NiceNIC — a registrar favored by threat actors (including Scattered Spider and The Com) due to its requirement for a Power of Attorney to process takedown requests — and domains leveraging Dynamic DNS services that create BPH-like abuse-resistant infrastructure. Any match warrants investigation for potential fraud-enabling infrastructure, C2 communication, or criminal hosting activity.

item.title: [DL-0179] Cloud Phone Behavioral Anomaly — Device-Environment Decorrelation Detection
item.description: Detects cloud phone behavioral anomalies indicative of industrial-scale dropper/mule account creation. Cloud phones — remote-access Android devices running genuine firmware on ARM hardware in data centers — pass hardware attestation and present authentic device signals, making them invisible to traditional emulator detection. This rule uses a composite scoring approach combining device-environment decorrelation signals: perpetual full battery, absence of accelerometer motion during active sessions, presence of VPN/proxy and vendor management apps, unusually high banking app density, and recent device first-seen dates. Group-IB reports cloud phone rental from $0.10/hour with pre-verified dropper accounts selling for $50–200 on darknet markets. UK APP fraud losses reached £485.2M in 2023 with dropper accounts as the top contributing factor.
