item.title: [DL-0180] Fake OTA Domain Pattern Detection — Domains Mimicking Booking.com/Expedia/Airbnb Registered < 30 Days
item.description: Detects web traffic to recently registered domains (< 30 days old) that mimic major Online Travel Agency brands (Booking.com, Expedia, Airbnb) using typosquatting, homoglyph substitution, or brand-adjacent naming patterns. These fake OTA domains are the primary infrastructure for travel booking fraud credential harvesting operations. NordVPN/Saily identified 4,344 active fake travel domains in 2026. Average domain lifespan is 18 days before takedown, making registration age the highest-signal detection feature. Domains serving payment form pages are critical-severity indicators.

item.title: [DL-0181] B4U Booking Velocity Anomaly — Same Payment Method Booking Across Multiple OTAs/Hotels in Rapid Succession
item.description: Detects Buy-for-You (B4U) booking fraud patterns where the same payment method is used to make travel bookings across multiple OTAs, airlines, or hotel chains within a 24-hour period, especially when bookings are made for different travelers. B4U operators use stolen payment credentials to purchase travel at legitimate platforms, then resell bookings at 30-60% of face value. Sumsub estimates B4U services generate $37B in annual travel fraud losses. The velocity of bookings across disparate merchants with mismatched traveler names is the hallmark detection signal.

item.title: [DL-0182] IRSF Traffic Spike Detection — Abnormal Call Volume to Premium-Rate International Numbers
item.description: Detects abnormal spikes in outbound call volume to premium-rate international number ranges, the hallmark indicator of International Revenue Share Fraud (IRSF). IRSF is the single largest telecom fraud category at $10.76B in annual losses (CFCA/TNS 2026). Fraudsters generate artificial traffic to premium-rate numbers where they hold revenue- sharing agreements, typically using compromised PBX systems or automated dialers. The detection uses z-score analysis against per-source baseline call volumes to premium-rate destinations, flagging when hourly volume exceeds 3 standard deviations. A compromised PBX can generate $50K-$500K in fraudulent charges within hours, making real-time detection critical.

item.title: [DL-0183] Wangiri Callback Velocity — High Volume of Short-Duration Outbound International Calls From Single Source
item.description: Detects Wangiri ("one-ring") fraud patterns where a high volume of short-duration (< 5 seconds) outbound international calls originate from a single source, indicating subscriber callbacks to premium-rate numbers. In a Wangiri scheme, fraudsters place brief inbound calls from premium-rate numbers to trigger victim callbacks. The callbacks connect to IVR systems or premium content lines that accumulate per-minute charges. This rule detects the callback side of the attack: clusters of brief outbound international calls from individual subscribers or PBX systems to premium-rate destinations. Average victim loss is $15-$50 per callback; aggregate campaign revenues reach $100K-$1M (Subex/Akamai).

item.title: [DL-0184] Telecom Subscription Velocity — Multiple New Service Activations From Same Identity/Device Within 30 Days
item.description: Detects subscription fraud patterns where the same identity or device IMEI is used to activate multiple new telecom service accounts within a 30-day window. Subscription fraud is the top concern for 53% of telecom executives (TransUnion 2025). Fraudsters use synthetic identities (TP-0003) with GenAI-generated KYC documents to open accounts across multiple carriers, acquiring subsidized flagship devices on installment plans with no payment intent. The multi-carrier activation pattern is the strongest detection signal, as legitimate customers rarely activate 3+ accounts across 2+ carriers in a 30-day period. Devices acquired through subscription fraud are resold at 60-80% of retail value on secondary markets.

item.title: [DL-0185] Premium SMS Billing Anomaly — Unauthorized Premium SMS Subscriptions Appearing on Accounts
item.description: Detects unauthorized premium SMS subscriptions (cramming) appearing on customer accounts without corresponding opt-in or consent records. Premium SMS cramming generates an estimated $1.5B in unauthorized consumer charges annually (CFCA/TNS 2026). Fraudsters add premium SMS shortcode subscriptions to accounts through compromised billing APIs, social engineering of carrier support staff, or malware-initiated WAP billing triggers. The key detection signal is premium SMS subscription records that lack a corresponding customer opt-in event. Multiple premium subscriptions appearing on the same account within a 30-day window without opt-in are high-confidence cramming indicators.

item.title: [DL-0186] Seller Impersonation Pattern — Property Sale Initiated by Non-Resident Owner of Vacant/Unencumbered Property With Recent Contact Info Changes
item.description: Detects the characteristic seller impersonation pattern in real estate title fraud: a property sale or title transfer is initiated on a vacant, unencumbered property where the owner is non-resident (mailing address differs from property address) and the owner's contact information has been recently changed. FBI data shows $16.6B in total real estate fraud losses (2024), with seller impersonation of vacant property owners as the fastest-growing subcategory. Fraudsters target vacant, mortgage-free properties because there is no occupant to notice and no lender monitoring the title. A risk score is computed from multiple indicators: non-resident owner, vacant property, unencumbered, recent contact changes, and below-market listing price.

item.title: [DL-0187] Fraudulent Deed Transfer Anomaly — Deed Recording With Document Metadata Anomalies (AI Generation Indicators) on Properties With No Prior Activity
item.description: Detects deed recordings that exhibit document metadata anomalies indicative of AI- generated or forged documents, particularly on properties with no recent prior recording activity. The detection combines document forensic signals (AI tool signatures in PDF metadata, rapid creation timestamps, font inconsistencies) with property-level risk factors (no prior recordings in 5 years, vacant status, unencumbered, non-resident owner). Entrust reports a 40% YoY increase in deepfake-related fraud attempts (2026), with AI-forged deeds, government IDs, and notary stamps as primary vectors in real estate title fraud. Notary commission validation is a critical check -- invalid or expired notary credentials are a high-confidence fraud indicator.

item.title: [DL-0188] Ghost Broker Policy Pattern — Multiple Policies with Disposable Contacts and Below-Market Premiums
item.description: Detects ghost broker activity by identifying intermediaries submitting multiple insurance policies using disposable contact details (temporary email addresses, prepaid phone numbers) with premiums significantly below market rates. Ghost broking victims increased 93% in 2025, with organized operators selling fake or fraudulently obtained policies at 30-60% below market rates. The combination of high policy volume, rotating disposable contacts, and below-market pricing is the hallmark pattern of ghost broker operations. City of London Police made arrests in May 2025 and IFED designated February 2026 as a ghost broking intensification month.

item.title: [DL-0189] Ghost Portal Infrastructure Detection — Fake Insurance Verification on Recently Registered Domains
item.description: Detects ghost portal infrastructure — fraudulent insurance verification websites deployed on recently registered domains that return valid-looking but unverifiable policy numbers. Ghost portals represent the evolution of ghost broking into a fraud-as-a-service model, where operators build and sell fake insurance verification platforms to other fraudsters. These portals are typically deployed on domains registered within the past 90 days, use insurance-related keywords, and mimic legitimate insurer verification workflows. Detection focuses on DNS queries and web traffic to recently registered domains containing insurance verification terminology.

item.title: [DL-0190] Chargeback Velocity Pattern — Serial Dispute Filing Across Merchants with Confirmed Delivery
item.description: Detects friendly fraud chargeback abuse by identifying cardholders with 3 or more chargebacks filed within a 90-day window across different merchants where delivery was confirmed for the original transactions. Friendly fraud represents 36% of all fraud, with 337 million chargebacks projected for 2026 costing USD 15.3 billion in the US. Chargeback abuse surged 233% between Q1 and Q3 2025. The combination of multi-merchant dispute filing with contradicting delivery evidence is a high-confidence indicator of first-party chargeback abuse rather than legitimate disputes. Merchants lose USD 4.61 for every USD 1.00 of friendly fraud.

item.title: [DL-0191] First-Party Dispute Anomaly — Chargeback with Delivery Confirmation, Device Match, and No Merchant Contact
item.description: Detects high-confidence friendly fraud by identifying chargebacks where three independent indicators contradict the dispute claim: (1) delivery was confirmed for the original order, (2) the device fingerprint filing the dispute matches the device used for the original purchase, and (3) no merchant contact was attempted before the chargeback was filed. The triple correlation of delivery evidence, device match, and merchant bypass is a strong signal that the cardholder is the original purchaser who received the goods and chose to file a chargeback rather than a legitimate return. 84% of consumers find chargebacks simpler than contacting merchants, creating systemic abuse of the dispute mechanism.

item.title: [DL-0192] Cookie Stuffing Detection — Affiliate Cookies Set Without Corresponding Click Events
item.description: Detects cookie stuffing — the most prevalent affiliate fraud technique (approximately 60% of cases) — by identifying affiliates that set tracking cookies in user browsers without corresponding user click events. Cookie stuffing uses hidden iframes, 1x1 pixel images, or JavaScript injection to drop affiliate cookies without the user's knowledge or intent. This steals attribution credit from legitimate affiliates and organic traffic, inflating the fraudulent affiliate's commission payments. Detection relies on the cookie-to-click ratio: legitimate affiliates typically have a ratio near 1:1, while cookie stuffers exhibit ratios of 5:1 or higher, or set cookies with zero associated clicks entirely. Global ad fraud is projected at USD 71 billion in 2025.

item.title: [DL-0193] Bot Traffic Behavioral Anomaly — Mechanical Consistency in Affiliate Session Metrics
item.description: Detects bot-generated affiliate traffic by identifying sessions with mechanical behavioral consistency — identical session durations, linear scroll patterns, and zero mouse movement variance — that indicate automated rather than human browsing. Bot networks account for approximately 40% of all click fraud, and AI-powered bots increasingly mimic individual human sessions. However, bot traffic still exhibits statistically detectable patterns at the population level: genuine human traffic has natural variance in behavioral metrics, while bot traffic — even sophisticated AI bots — produces distributions with anomalously low standard deviation. This rule analyzes session-level behavioral distributions per affiliate to detect mechanical consistency at the aggregate level.

item.title: [DL-0194] AI-Generated Claims Document Detection — Metadata Anomalies and Generation Tool Signatures
item.description: Detects AI-generated or AI-altered insurance claims documents by analyzing metadata anomalies including GAN artifacts, inconsistent EXIF data, and AI generation tool signatures. An estimated 25-30% of insurance claims now involve some form of GenAI-altered content. This rule targets the document forensics layer: photos submitted without legitimate camera metadata, documents with AI tool signatures in creation metadata, images with frequency domain anomalies characteristic of GAN generation, and GPS coordinates that contradict the claimed loss location. The insurance fraud detection market is growing from USD 7.5B to USD 9.13B reflecting industry investment in these countermeasures. Debener et al. (2023) demonstrate that XGBoost and isolation forests provide complementary detection approaches for anomalous claims.

item.title: [DL-0195] Deepfake Vehicle Damage Photo Pattern — Pixel Artifacts, Lighting Inconsistencies, and AI Generation Indicators
item.description: Detects deepfake vehicle damage photos in insurance claims by analyzing pixel-level artifacts, lighting and shadow inconsistencies, and metadata indicating AI image generation tools. AI-generated vehicle damage photos represent an acute threat to auto insurance claims processing, as generative AI can produce realistic collision, hail, and vandalism damage images that bypass visual inspection by claims adjusters. Detection relies on computer vision analysis: GAN-generated images exhibit characteristic pixel artifacts at damage boundaries, physically impossible lighting/shadow combinations, and frequency domain signatures distinct from camera-captured photos. This rule targets vehicle-specific claims (collision, comprehensive, vandalism) and correlates image forensics scores with claim characteristics.

item.title: [DL-0196] Stablecoin Flow to CEX via Hot Wallet Sweep Pattern
item.description: Detects the 2-hop hot wallet sweep pattern used in industrialized stablecoin laundering pipelines: illicit or high-risk funds flow from a flagged/suspicious address to a centralized exchange (CEX) deposit address (hop 1), which is then automatically swept into the exchange institutional hot wallet (hop 2). Confirming both hops confirms the exchange relationship and receipt of flagged funds. This pattern was documented by ICIJ in the Huione Group investigation, where at least $408 million flowed to Binance and $226 million to OKX via TRON/USDT through this exact mechanism. The detection leverages publicly available exchange Proof-of-Reserves (PoR) address lists and Arkham Intelligence illicit wallet tags to attribute both source risk and destination exchange. TRON/USDT is the primary monitoring surface given its dominance as the SE Asian fraud compound laundering rail.

item.title: [DL-0197] Crypto-to-Cash Desk — Ephemeral Wallet and Unlicensed OTC Indicators
item.description: Detects crypto-to-cash desk operations that convert USDT to physical currency with minimal or no KYC, generating fresh wallet addresses per transaction to defeat blockchain tracing. These unlicensed OTC operations represent the final monetization layer in stablecoin laundering pipelines, bridging the gap between on-chain cryptocurrency and usable physical cash. ICIJ investigators documented such operations in Dubai and Eastern European cities during the Coin Laundry investigation, with one desk processing $2 million in volume over 10 days on the TRON network alone — and critically, that desk did not appear in any major blockchain analytics provider attribution database (Chainalysis, TRM, Elliptic). The detection targets ephemeral wallets (< 7 days old, < 3 prior transactions) receiving USDT from multiple distinct sources on TRON, where the destination wallet is not attributed in any known analytics or exchange Proof-of-Reserves database.

item.title: [DL-0198] Shell Company Address Concentration as Fraud Infrastructure Indicator
item.description: Detects abnormal concentration of corporate registrations at a single registered address as an indicator of shell company infrastructure used for fraud, money laundering, or beneficial ownership obfuscation. The ICIJ/OpenCorporates investigation of Wyoming documented that 40% of all Wyoming LLCs are registered to just two buildings in Sheridan, WY, with a 30% spike in LLC registrations in 2023 alone. Wyoming now surpasses Delaware in companies registered per capita. Wyoming LLC services are actively marketed in Cyprus, Singapore, and other offshore jurisdictions as tax avoidance and asset-shielding vehicles. Millions in PPP loan fraud were traced to shell companies registered at a single Wyoming storefront address. The Corporate Transparency Act beneficial ownership registry — catalyzed by the FinCEN Files investigation — was effectively gutted in 2025 when the Trump Administration suspended all enforcement and deleted previously submitted data, removing the primary countermeasure against shell company opacity in the United States. This rule targets the recon phase (P1) where fraud infrastructure is established through mass corporate registration at concentrated addresses.

item.title: [DL-0199] ASN Reputation Clustering — High Abuse-Density Autonomous Systems
item.description: Detects network traffic to or from IP addresses within autonomous systems (ASNs) that exhibit high abuse density — defined as a concentration of abuse reports, malware hosting, and fraud-associated domains relative to total IP allocation. BPH operators concentrate on ASNs with high abuse-to-IP ratios due to their resistance to takedown. ASN-level reputation clustering is more resilient to infrastructure rotation than individual IP blocking, as operators rotate IPs within the same ASN. Sourced from Flare Academy BPH Webinar and Recorded Future TAE provider intelligence.

item.title: [DL-0200] Infrastructure Rotation Velocity — Rapid DNS IP Changes Within BPH Networks
item.description: Detects domains exhibiting rapid IP address rotation characteristic of bulletproof hosting infrastructure management. BPH operators rotate IP addresses every 24-72 hours to evade blocklists, with emergency rotation following IOC publication. A domain resolving to 4+ unique IPs within 7 days — particularly when those IPs span multiple TAE provider ASNs — is a strong indicator of managed BPH infrastructure rotation. This detection complements static IP blocklists by identifying the rotation behavior itself. Sourced from Flare Academy BPH Webinar and Cybercrime Diaries BPH landscape analysis.

item.title: [DL-0201] AiTM Antibot Cloaking Detection — Divergent Content by Client Type
item.description: Detects phishing pages that serve different content to automated scanners versus human visitors — a key evasion technique used by PhaaS platforms including Bluekit, Tycoon 2FA, and NakedPages. Antibot cloaking typically returns benign content (blank pages, Wikipedia redirects, legitimate-looking sites) to known scanner User-Agents, IP ranges associated with security vendors, and headless browsers, while serving the actual phishing page to real victims. Detection compares HTTP responses for the same URL across different client profiles. Sourced from Bluekit PhaaS TI report (CrimsonVector, March 2026).

item.title: [DL-0202] Browser Fingerprint Spoofing — User-Agent Inconsistency in Authentication Flow
item.description: Detects authentication sessions where the User-Agent string changes between sequential authentication steps — a strong indicator of AiTM proxy-based session hijacking. Bluekit advertises "full 2FA support with emulation/spoofing of geolocation and browser information," and Sneaky 2FA exhibits an "impossible device shift" where Safari/iOS is used for login but Edge/Windows for session resume. When a legitimate user authenticates, the User-Agent remains consistent throughout the flow. AiTM proxies may inject different User-Agents at different stages due to proxy architecture or deliberate fingerprint spoofing. Sourced from Bluekit PhaaS TI report and Sekoia TDR Sneaky 2FA analysis.

item.title: [DL-0203] Crypto Laundering Service Fee Pattern — Percentage-Based Deduction on Transfers
item.description: Detects cryptocurrency transfer patterns consistent with laundering service fee structures. Illicit crypto exchange services charge 2.8%-8.5% base fees plus a 4% "dirty funds" surcharge, resulting in outbound amounts that are consistently 93-97% of inbound amounts. When a wallet receives cryptocurrency and forwards approximately 93-97% to another address within 24 hours — retaining 3-7% as a service fee — this is a strong indicator of a crypto mixing or cashout service. The retained percentage serves as the service operator's commission. Sourced from Cybercrime Diaries undercover exchange contact research (June 2025).

item.title: [DL-0204] Stablecoin-to-Decentralized-Stablecoin Swap Velocity
item.description: Detects when a wallet receives USDT/USDC and swaps to decentralized stablecoins (DAI, sDAI, LUSD, RAI) via a DEX within 24 hours, particularly when the source wallet has elevated risk scores. The IRGC's documented USDT-to-DAI shift after mid-2025 Tether freezes is the direct intelligence basis. Centralized stablecoins can be frozen by issuers; swapping to decentralized alternatives defeats this control.

item.title: [DL-0205] Wrapped Stablecoin Bridge Transfer from High-Risk Source
item.description: Detects stablecoin bridge transactions where USDT/USDC is wrapped through bridge protocols to create wrapped representations (wUSDT, wUSDC) on destination chains, and the source address has elevated risk indicators or recent exposure to sanctioned addresses. Bridging defeats the original issuer's freeze capability on the destination chain, making this a key laundering technique for sanctioned actors.

item.title: [DL-0206] Rapid Wallet Fan-Out Exceeding 100 Wallets Post-Theft
item.description: Detects when a single wallet or cluster distributes funds across 100+ new wallets within 48 hours following a large-value transfer (>$1M). Directly models the DPRK Bybit laundering pattern where PRESSURE CHOLLIMA distributed stolen funds across 125,000+ Ethereum wallets. Existing DL-0196 and DL-0197 cover CEX off-ramp detection; this rule covers the upstream distancing and layering phase.

item.title: [DL-0207] Micro-Splitting Stablecoin Donations to Rotating Wallets
item.description: Detect patterns of small-value stablecoin transfers ($10-$500) sent to wallets that are used only once or twice before rotating to new addresses. Models the ISIL/Al-Qaeda donation solicitation pattern: rotating wallet addresses, micro-splitting, and multi-hop transfers designed to evade transaction monitoring thresholds.

item.title: [DL-0208] New gTLD Domain Registration Burst with Phishing Characteristics
item.description: Detect bulk domain registrations (5+ in 24h from same registrant/nameserver) on high-abuse gTLDs (.TOP, .BOND, .XYZ, .SHOP, .XIN, .CFD, .LOL) with brand-keyword presence, domain age < 7 days, and low registration cost. Interisle found 37% of phishing domains were bulk-registered and new gTLDs accounted for 51% of all phishing domains.

item.title: [DL-0209] Legitimate PaaS Subdomain Hosting Phishing Content
item.description: Detect URLs hosted on known PaaS free subdomain services (*.pages.dev, *.webflow.io, *.vercel.app, *.github.io, *.gitbook.io, *.workers.dev, *.r2.dev) that contain financial brand keywords or trigger phishing heuristics. These subdomains inherit the PaaS provider's domain reputation, bypassing domain-age and reputation filters commonly used in fraud detection.

item.title: [DL-0210] IDN Homograph Domain Targeting Crypto Brands
item.description: Detect DNS queries or URL accesses to internationalized domain names (IDN/punycode with xn-- prefix) that visually resemble crypto brand domains (bitpay, coinbase, metamask, phantom, pancakeswap, uniswap, etc.). Interisle documented 2,655 IDN homograph phishing domains with significant crypto brand targeting.

item.title: [DL-0211] Fake CAPTCHA Campaign Redirect Chain Detection
item.description: Detect web access patterns consistent with fake CAPTCHA campaigns: user visits a page with CAPTCHA verification UI, is instructed to copy/execute clipboard content (PowerShell, cmd, mshta), which triggers malware or stealer download. CrowdStrike documented a +563% increase in fake CAPTCHA campaigns in 2025. Used by BRASH SPIDER (Doshell Stealer) and COOKIE SPIDER (SHAMOS).

item.title: [DL-0212] Elder Account — Large Cash Withdrawal with Crypto ATM Deposit Indicators
item.description: Detects the elder-targeted crypto ATM fraud pattern where victims aged 60+ make large cash withdrawals with no corresponding deposit or transfer activity within 48 hours — a strong indicator that funds were deposited at a crypto ATM/kiosk under the direction of a scammer. FBI IC3 2025 data shows 6,188 crypto ATM complaints and $257 million in losses from victims aged 60+ (66% of all crypto ATM fraud losses). The 48-hour gap between bank withdrawal and lack of corresponding activity represents the detection window before funds become irrecoverable on-chain. This rule targets the P4 execution phase where bank-side intervention can still prevent loss.

item.title: [DL-0213] Unusual Large Cash Withdrawal with Precious Metals Merchant Transaction
item.description: Detects the gold courier scam pattern where victims — predominantly elderly — make large cash withdrawals or wire transfers to precious metals merchants with no prior history of such transactions. FBI IC3 2025 documented 725 gold courier complaints with $311.8 million in losses, yielding an extraordinary average of ~$430,000 per victim. Victims are typically directed by government impersonation callers to purchase physical gold as "asset protection," which is then collected by couriers. The precious metals MCC codes (5094 for precious stones/metals, 5944 for jewelry/watch/clock stores) serve as the primary detection signal when combined with customer age and transaction history anomalies.

item.title: [DL-0214] Post-Fraud Victim Payment to Newly Registered Legal or Recovery Entity
item.description: Detects recovery fraud patterns where victims of prior fraud are targeted by fictitious law firms or recovery companies promising to retrieve lost funds. FBI IC3 2025 reported 10,516 recovery scam complaints with $1.4 billion in losses — making recovery fraud one of the largest IC3 loss categories. PSA250813 (August 2025) specifically warned about fictitious law firms targeting cryptocurrency scam victims. This rule identifies the characteristic pattern: a customer with a recent fraud complaint making payments to a newly established entity with legal or recovery terminology in the payee name. The 180-day lookback window accounts for IC3 data showing longer re-targeting timelines than previously estimated.

item.title: [DL-0215] Multiple Unrelated Customers Depositing to Same Novel Beneficiary — Investment Club Pattern
item.description: Detects investment club scam patterns where multiple unrelated victims deposit funds to the same fraudulent beneficiary within a short time window. FBI IC3 2025 documented approximately 1,600 investment club complaints with $160 million in losses, and PSA250703 specifically warned about fraudulent investment clubs on social media and messaging apps. The cluster deposit pattern — five or more unique, unrelated customers sending to the same novel beneficiary within 14 days — distinguishes investment club scams from 1:1 pig butchering (TP-0017) where victims typically deposit to unique beneficiary accounts. The group-based nature creates a detectable convergence signal absent from individual targeting schemes.

item.title: [DL-0216] Government Impersonation — Multi-Channel Payment Under Duress Indicators
item.description: Detects government impersonation APP fraud by identifying payments with government agency references made via crypto, wire, or prepaid channels to non-historical payees. FBI IC3 2025 reported $797.9 million in losses from 32,424 government impersonation complaints — an 87% increase in complaints and 97% increase in losses from 2024. The payment channel distribution is distinctive: Cryptocurrency 40%, Wire Transfer/ACH 21%, Prepaid card/Gift card 15%, Cash 14%. This rule targets payment references containing government agency names or legal terminology from customers with no prior government- related payment history, as legitimate government payments follow established patterns and channels.

item.title: [DL-0217] AI-Enhanced BEC — Payment Request Behavioral Divergence from Sender Baseline
item.description: Detects AI-enhanced business email compromise by identifying wire transfer requests where the communication pattern diverges significantly from the sender's established baseline. FBI IC3 2025 reported $30 million in losses from AI-enabled BEC where chat generators created official-sounding emails mimicking company executives and voice cloning was used for wire authorization requests. AI-generated BEC content, while linguistically fluent, often lacks the sender's authentic communication patterns — writing style, formality level, time-of-day preferences, typical request amounts, and approval workflows. This rule targets Phase 3 (Positioning) where the fraudulent request is crafted and delivered, before the wire transfer is executed.
